KRaft (Section 2.3) raised the practical limit per cluster considerably compared to ZooKeeper, but thousands of tiny, unused partitions still waste resources and slow down failover and rebalances.

**Example: how keys map to partitions, and what happens when you add partitions**

In Java, you can reproduce the default partitioner's choice with Kafka's own utility methods:

```java
import org.apache.kafka.common.utils.Utils;

byte[] keyBytes = "CUST-77".getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
int numPartitions = 6;
// The same formula the default partitioner uses for non-null keys
int partition = Utils.toPositive(Utils.murmur2(keyBytes)) % numPartitions;
System.out.println("CUST-77 -> partition " + partition);
```

This Python simulation (using CRC32 as a stand-in hash) shows how many keys move when a topic grows from 3 to 4 partitions:

```python
import zlib

keys = [f"CUST-{i}" for i in range(1, 1001)]

def partition_for(key: str, num_partitions: int) -> int:
    return zlib.crc32(key.encode()) % num_partitions   # hash(key) mod N, like Kafka

before = {k: partition_for(k, 3) for k in keys}
after = {k: partition_for(k, 4) for k in keys}

moved = sum(1 for k in keys if before[k] != after[k])
print(f"{moved} of {len(keys)} keys changed partition")   # roughly 75% of keys move
```

A cross-language pitfall: `librdkafka`-based clients (Python `confluent-kafka`, Go, .NET, and others) default to a **different** hash (`consistent_random`, based on CRC32) than the Java client's murmur2. If Java and Python services both produce keyed records to the same topic, set `"partitioner": "murmur2_random"` in the librdkafka clients so the same key lands in the same partition.

```python
from confluent_kafka import Producer

producer = Producer({
    "bootstrap.servers": "localhost:9092",
    "partitioner": "murmur2_random",   # match the Java client's key -> partition mapping
})
```

**Key Takeaways**

- A partition is an independent, ordered log. A topic is a set of partitions.
- Partitions are the unit of parallelism, ordering, storage distribution, and replication.
- Records with the same key go to the same partition, so they keep their order. There is no ordering across partitions.
- The partition count can only increase, and increasing it remaps most keys. Plan it up front for keyed topics.
- Clients in different languages may hash keys differently. Align partitioners when multiple producers share a topic.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. (Beginner) A topic has 4 partitions and a consumer group with 4 consumers is falling behind. What is the maximum number of consumers in that group that can do useful work, and what must change to scale further?
> 2. (Intermediate) Modify the Python simulation to grow from 6 to 12 partitions. What fraction of keys move? Why is doubling the partition count gentler than going from 6 to 7 for some keys, and why does it still break ordering guarantees during the transition?
> 3. **Interview question:** "How does Kafka guarantee ordering, and what would you do if the business requires all events for a customer to be processed in order?" *Hint: consider what the key determines, and what could reorder records inside a single partition on the producer side (Chapter 4, `max.in.flight.requests` and idempotence).*

#### Offsets

**Theory**

Each partition is a log, and every record in it has a position: its **offset**. An offset is a 64-bit integer, assigned by the partition leader when the record is appended, that increases with each record. Offsets are **per partition**: offset 42 in partition 0 and offset 42 in partition 1 are unrelated records. So a record's full address is the tuple `(topic, partition, offset)`.

Why does this matter? Because Kafka does not track which records each consumer has read. The *consumer* tracks its own position as a single number per partition. That is what makes Kafka cheap to read from: thousands of consumers can read the same partition, and the broker stores no per-message delivery state at all.

> Analogy: an offset is a page number in a book that never stops growing. Each reader uses their own bookmark. Closing the book and reopening it later, you just turn to your bookmark. Anyone can move their bookmark back to reread a chapter, and doing so does not affect other readers.

**Important offsets in a partition**

```text
Partition "orders-0"

      +-----+-----+-----+-----+-----+-----+-----+-----+-----+
      | 100 | 101 | ... | 107 | 108 | 109 | 110 | 111 | 112 |
      +-----+-----+-----+-----+-----+-----+-----+-----+-----+
         ^                       ^                       ^     ^
         |                       |                       |     +---- log end offset (LEO) = 113
         |                       |                       +---------- high watermark (HW) = 112
         |                       +---------------------------------- committed offset, group "billing" = 108
         +---------------------------------------------------------- log start offset = 100 (0-99 deleted)

  100-107 : already processed by group "billing"
  108-111 : readable but not yet processed -> lag = 112 - 108 = 4
  112     : on the leader, not yet on all in-sync replicas -> invisible to consumers
```

| Offset | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Log start offset | The oldest offset still available. Earlier records were removed by retention or compaction. |
| Committed offset | The *next* offset a consumer group will read after a restart. It is stored in `__consumer_offsets`. |
| Current position | The next offset the consumer will fetch in its current session (may be ahead of the committed offset). |
| High watermark (HW) | The offset up to which all in-sync replicas have the data. Consumers can only read below it (Section 2.4). |
| Log end offset (LEO) | The offset the next appended record will receive. |
| Consumer lag | High watermark minus committed offset: how far behind a group is. |

A common off-by-one source: the committed offset is the offset of the **next record to read**, not the last record processed. If you processed offset 107, you commit 108.

**Offsets are not always contiguous**

Offsets always increase, but consumers can see gaps:

- **Compaction** removes older records for a key, leaving holes.
- **Transactions** write control records (commit/abort markers) that take an offset but are never returned to applications.

So never assume `next offset = current offset + 1` when computing counts. Use offsets as positions, not as record counts.

**What happens when the committed offset is invalid**

When a group has no committed offset (it is new) or its committed offset was deleted by retention, the consumer setting `auto.offset.reset` decides where to start:

| Value | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `latest` (default) | Start at the end, reading only new records |
| `earliest` | Start at the log start offset, reading all retained history |
| `none` | Throw an exception and let the application decide |

**Seeking: moving the bookmark yourself**

Because the position is just a number, consumers can rewind or skip ahead on purpose: `seek()` to a specific offset, `seekToBeginning()`, `seekToEnd()`, or `offsetsForTimes()` to find the first offset at or after a timestamp. This is how you replay a day of events after fixing a bug.

**Example: inspecting and moving offsets**

```java
TopicPartition tp = new TopicPartition("orders", 0);
consumer.assign(List.of(tp));                    // manual assignment, no group rebalancing

// Where does the log start and end?
long start = consumer.beginningOffsets(List.of(tp)).get(tp);
long end   = consumer.endOffsets(List.of(tp)).get(tp);   // HW for read_uncommitted consumers
System.out.printf("available offsets: [%d, %d)%n", start, end);

// Replay everything since yesterday at 00:00 UTC
long ts = LocalDate.now(ZoneOffset.UTC).minusDays(1).atStartOfDay(ZoneOffset.UTC).toInstant().toEpochMilli();
OffsetAndTimestamp found = consumer.offsetsForTimes(Map.of(tp, ts)).get(tp);
if (found != null) {
    consumer.seek(tp, found.offset());           // move this consumer's position
} else {
    consumer.seekToEnd(List.of(tp));             // no record that new: nothing to replay
}

for (ConsumerRecord<String, String> rec : consumer.poll(Duration.ofSeconds(1))) {
    process(rec);
    // Commit "next to read" = last processed + 1
    consumer.commitSync(Map.of(tp, new OffsetAndMetadata(rec.offset() + 1)));
}
```

Checking a group's committed offsets and lag from the command line:

```bash
bin/kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --describe --group billing
```

```text
GROUP    TOPIC   PARTITION  CURRENT-OFFSET  LOG-END-OFFSET  LAG  CONSUMER-ID          HOST        CLIENT-ID
billing  orders  0          108             112             4    consumer-billing-1   /10.0.0.5   consumer-billing-1
billing  orders  1          5530            5530            0    consumer-billing-2   /10.0.0.6   consumer-billing-2
```

Here `CURRENT-OFFSET` is the committed offset. Despite its name, the `LOG-END-OFFSET` column shows the offset consumers can read up to (the high watermark), which is why lag computed from it reflects only readable data.

**Key Takeaways**

- An offset is a per-partition, increasing 64-bit position. `(topic, partition, offset)` uniquely identifies a record.
- Consumers own their position. The broker keeps no per-message delivery state, which makes fan-out and replay cheap.
- The committed offset is the next record to read (last processed + 1) and is stored in `__consumer_offsets`.
- Offsets can have gaps (compaction, transaction markers). Do not use them as record counts.
- `auto.offset.reset` applies only when there is no valid committed offset. `seek` and `offsetsForTimes` let you replay deliberately.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. (Beginner) A consumer processes records at offsets 40, 41, and 42 in partition 3, then commits. Which offset should it commit, and what record will it read first after a restart?
> 2. (Intermediate) A group was offline for 10 days on a topic with 7-day retention. Its committed offset is 5,000, but the log start offset is now 90,000. What happens on restart with `auto.offset.reset=latest`, with `earliest`, and with `none`? Which records are lost to this group in each case?
> 3. **Interview question:** "Why can Kafka support thousands of consumers on one topic while a traditional broker struggles with per-message acknowledgments?" *Hint: compare the state the broker must store and update for each approach.*

#### Segments and Log Files

**Theory**

If each partition were one ever-growing file, deleting old data would mean rewriting the file, and finding a record by offset would mean scanning gigabytes. Kafka avoids both problems by splitting each partition's log into **segments**: a sequence of files, each covering a contiguous range of offsets.

- Exactly one segment per partition is **active**: new records are appended only to it.
- When the active segment reaches a size or age limit, it is **rolled**: closed, and a new active segment is opened.
- Closed segments are immutable. Retention deletes them **whole**, which is just a file deletion and is very cheap.

> Analogy: a diary written across numbered notebooks. You only write in the current notebook. When it is full, you start a new one. To throw away old entries, you discard entire old notebooks rather than tearing out pages. Each notebook has a small index card at the front saying roughly which page each date starts on.

**What is inside a partition directory**

Each partition replica is a directory named `<topic>-<partition>` under one of the broker's `log.dirs`. Each segment is a group of files sharing a name, which is the segment's **base offset** (its first offset) padded to 20 digits:

```text
/var/lib/kafka/data/orders-0/
|-- 00000000000000000000.log          <- segment 1: offsets 0 .. 368768 (closed)
|-- 00000000000000000000.index        <- sparse offset index for segment 1
|-- 00000000000000000000.timeindex    <- sparse timestamp index for segment 1
|-- 00000000000000368769.log          <- segment 2: offsets 368769 .. (ACTIVE, being appended)
|-- 00000000000000368769.index
|-- 00000000000000368769.timeindex
|-- 00000000000000368769.snapshot     <- producer state snapshot (idempotence, Chapter 8)
|-- leader-epoch-checkpoint           <- leader epoch -> start offset history (Section 2.4)
`-- partition.metadata                <- topic ID for this partition
```

| File | Contents | Entry Format |
|---|---|---|
| `.log` | Record batches, exactly as received from the producer | Variable-length batches |
| `.index` | Offset to byte position in the `.log` file | 8 bytes: relative offset (4) + file position (4) |
| `.timeindex` | Timestamp to offset | 12 bytes: timestamp (8) + relative offset (4) |
| `.txnindex` | Aborted transactions in this segment (only if transactions are used) | Used by `read_committed` consumers |
| `.snapshot` | Producer IDs and sequence numbers | Used to rebuild idempotence state quickly |

**Sparse indexes**

The indexes do not contain every offset. By default, the broker adds an index entry roughly every 4 KB of log data (`index.interval.bytes=4096`). Finding offset *N* therefore takes three steps:

```text
Find offset 368,900 in orders-0

1. Pick the segment: binary search over base offsets in memory
     [0, 368769, 737538, ...]  ->  368769 <= 368900 < 737538  ->  segment 368769

2. Search that segment's .index (memory-mapped) for the greatest entry <= 368900
     relative offset 131 (= 368900 - 368769)
     .index: ... (96 -> pos 61440) (128 -> pos 81920) (160 -> pos 102400) ...
                                    ^ closest entry at or below 131

3. Scan the .log file forward from byte 81920 until offset 368900 is reached (at most ~4 KB)
```

Storing *relative* offsets (offset minus base offset) in 4 bytes keeps index entries small, and memory-mapping the index files means lookups usually hit RAM.

**When a segment rolls**

| Setting (Broker / Topic) | Default | Rolls When |
|---|---|---|
| `log.segment.bytes` / `segment.bytes` | 1 GiB | The active segment reaches this size |
| `log.roll.hours` / `segment.ms` | 7 days | The active segment is this old |
| `log.index.size.max.bytes` / `segment.index.bytes` | 10 MiB | The offset or time index file is full |

**Why segments matter for retention**

Retention works on closed segments only. A segment is deleted when its newest record is older than `retention.ms` (or when the partition exceeds `retention.bytes`). The active segment is never deleted. This has a surprising consequence: on a low-traffic topic with `retention.ms` of 1 hour but the default 7-day `segment.ms`, data can live for about a week because the active segment has not rolled yet. Lowering `segment.ms` fixes this, at the cost of more files.

Chapter 7 covers segment internals, compaction, and tiered storage in depth.

**Example: looking inside a segment and simulating the lookup**

Kafka ships a tool that decodes segment files:

```bash
bin/kafka-dump-log.sh --print-data-log \
  --files /var/lib/kafka/data/orders-0/00000000000000000000.log
```

```text
Dumping /var/lib/kafka/data/orders-0/00000000000000000000.log
Log starting offset: 0
baseOffset: 0 lastOffset: 2 count: 3 baseSequence: 0 lastSequence: 2 producerId: 1000
  producerEpoch: 0 partitionLeaderEpoch: 0 isTransactional: false isControl: false
  position: 0 CreateTime: 1761210942120 size: 196 magic: 2 compresscodec: none crc: 2415896217 isvalid: true
| offset: 0 CreateTime: 1761210942120 keySize: 7 valueSize: 36 sequence: 0 headerKeys: [trace-id] key: CUST-77 payload: {"orderId":"ORD-1042","total":39.98}
| offset: 1 CreateTime: 1761210942121 keySize: 7 valueSize: 36 sequence: 1 headerKeys: [trace-id] key: CUST-12 payload: {"orderId":"ORD-1043","total":12.50}
...
```

(Output abridged.) Notice that metadata is stored once per **batch** (`baseOffset`, `producerId`, `crc`), while each record carries only small deltas.

A Python model of the three-step lookup:

```python
from bisect import bisect_right

# Step 1 data: base offsets of each segment, kept sorted in memory by the broker
segment_bases = [0, 368_769, 737_538]

# Step 2 data: sparse index per segment -> list of (relative_offset, byte_position)
sparse_index = {
    368_769: [(0, 0), (32, 20_480), (64, 40_960), (96, 61_440), (128, 81_920), (160, 102_400)],
}

def locate(offset: int) -> tuple[int, int]:
    # 1. Find the segment: greatest base offset <= target
    seg = segment_bases[bisect_right(segment_bases, offset) - 1]
    # 2. Find the greatest index entry <= relative target
    entries = sparse_index[seg]
    rel = offset - seg
    i = bisect_right([e[0] for e in entries], rel) - 1
    start_pos = entries[i][1]
    # 3. The broker would now scan the .log file forward from start_pos
    return seg, start_pos

print(locate(368_900))   # (368769, 81920): open segment 368769, scan from byte 81920
```

**Key Takeaways**

- Each partition is stored as a series of segment files. Only the active segment is written to.
- Segment files are named by their base offset. Each `.log` has a sparse `.index` (offset to position) and `.timeindex` (time to offset).
- Lookups are a binary search over segments, then over a memory-mapped sparse index, then a short sequential scan.
- Segments roll by size, age, or full index. Retention deletes whole closed segments and never the active one.
- `segment.ms` and `segment.bytes` affect how precisely retention is enforced and how many files a broker must manage.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. (Beginner) A partition directory contains `00000000000000000000.log`, `00000000000000052000.log`, and `00000000000000104000.log`. Which file contains offset 60,123? Which file is most likely the active segment?
> 2. (Intermediate) A topic receives 10 records per hour and has `retention.ms=3600000` (1 hour) with default segment settings. A compliance officer finds 5-day-old records. Explain why, and propose a configuration change, including its trade-off.
> 3. **Interview question:** "How does Kafka find a record by offset quickly without an index entry for every record?" *Hint: describe the three lookup steps and explain why a full index would be wasteful given how consumers typically read.*

<a id="22-brokers-and-clusters"></a>
### 2.2 Brokers and Clusters

This section moves from data structures to the servers that host them: what a broker does, how brokers form a cluster, which node coordinates the cluster, how clients find brokers, and how replicas are spread across failure domains.

#### Broker Role and Responsibilities

**Theory**

A **broker** is a single Kafka server process. It is "just" a JVM process that owns some disks and listens on some ports, but it does a lot of work:

| Responsibility | What It Means |
|---|---|
| Storage | Hosts partition replicas as segment files in its `log.dirs`, and enforces retention and compaction |
| Serving writes | Accepts `Produce` requests for partitions it **leads**, appends them, and acknowledges according to `acks` |
| Serving reads | Answers `Fetch` requests from consumers (and from follower replicas on other brokers) |
| Replication | Acts as a follower for partitions led elsewhere by fetching from their leaders |
| Metadata | Answers `Metadata` requests so clients learn which broker leads which partition |
| Coordination | Hosts coordinators: the **group coordinator** (consumer groups, offset commits), the **transaction coordinator** (Chapter 8), and the **share coordinator** (share groups) |

A key design choice: **a broker only serves reads and writes for partitions it leads** (followers can serve reads when follower fetching is enabled, see Rack Awareness). Clients therefore talk directly to the right broker for each partition. No central router sits in the data path, so adding brokers adds capacity almost linearly.

> Analogy: a broker is like a branch of a library network. Each branch holds some of the collection (partitions), lends out what it holds (serves fetches), accepts donations for its own shelves (produces), and keeps photocopies of some books held at other branches (follower replicas) in case one branch burns down.

**Brokers are deliberately "dumb"**

Compared to traditional message brokers, Kafka brokers do very little per message:

- No per-message acknowledgments or redelivery tracking (consumers track offsets).
- No routing rules, filtering, or priority queues.
- No payload parsing: batches are written and served as opaque bytes, often straight from the page cache to the socket (zero-copy).

This "smart client, simple broker" split is the source of much of Kafka's throughput.

**Inside a broker: the request path**

```text
            clients / other brokers
                     |
                     v
          +---------------------+
          |  Acceptor thread    |   one per listener: accepts TCP connections
          +---------------------+
                     |
                     v
          +---------------------+
          |  Network threads    |   num.network.threads (default 3): read requests,
          |  (processors)       |   write responses
          +---------------------+
                     |  request queue
                     v
          +---------------------+
          |  I/O threads        |   num.io.threads (default 8): append to log,
          |  (request handlers) |   read from log, update metadata
          +---------------------+
              |            |
              |            v
              |    +----------------+   requests that must wait: acks=all produce
              |    |   Purgatory    |   (until followers catch up), fetches with
              |    +----------------+   fetch.min.bytes not yet satisfied
              v            |
          response queue <-+
                     |
                     v
          network thread -> client
```

You rarely tune these threads early on, but knowing the path helps you read metrics like `RequestQueueTimeMs` and `RequestHandlerAvgIdlePercent` when diagnosing slowness (Chapters 12 and 16).

**Listeners**

A broker can expose several **listeners**, each a named endpoint with its own security protocol. Separating them lets you, for example, use plaintext inside a private network and TLS with authentication for external clients.

| Setting | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `listeners` | Interfaces and ports the broker binds to |
| `advertised.listeners` | Addresses the broker tells clients to use (must be reachable by them) |
| `listener.security.protocol.map` | Maps each listener name to `PLAINTEXT`, `SSL`, `SASL_PLAINTEXT`, or `SASL_SSL` |
| `inter.broker.listener.name` | Listener used for broker-to-broker replication |
| `controller.listener.names` | Listener(s) used to talk to the KRaft controllers |

**Example: a broker configuration (KRaft mode)**

```properties
# ----- Identity and role -----
process.roles=broker                     # this node only serves data (see Cluster Topology)
node.id=4                                # unique across ALL nodes in the cluster

# ----- How to reach the controllers (Section 2.3) -----
controller.quorum.bootstrap.servers=ctrl1:9093,ctrl2:9093,ctrl3:9093
controller.listener.names=CONTROLLER

# ----- Listeners -----
listeners=INTERNAL://0.0.0.0:9092,EXTERNAL://0.0.0.0:9094
advertised.listeners=INTERNAL://broker4.kafka.internal:9092,EXTERNAL://kafka4.example.com:9094
listener.security.protocol.map=INTERNAL:PLAINTEXT,EXTERNAL:SASL_SSL,CONTROLLER:PLAINTEXT
inter.broker.listener.name=INTERNAL      # replication traffic stays on the private network

# ----- Storage -----
log.dirs=/var/lib/kafka/data-1,/var/lib/kafka/data-2   # several disks (JBOD) are allowed

# ----- Defaults for new topics -----
num.partitions=6
default.replication.factor=3
min.insync.replicas=2
auto.create.topics.enable=false
```

**Key Takeaways**

- A broker is a Kafka server that stores partition replicas and serves produce, fetch, and metadata requests.
- Clients send data directly to the leader of each partition. No central router exists, so the cluster scales horizontally.
- Brokers do little per message (no acks per message, no routing, no parsing), which enables high throughput.
- Brokers also host the group, transaction, and share coordinators.
- Listeners separate traffic by network and security protocol. `advertised.listeners` must be reachable by clients.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. (Beginner) List four kinds of requests a broker handles, and say which ones come from producers, consumers, and other brokers.
> 2. (Intermediate) Draw the path of an `acks=all` produce request through a broker's threads. Explain why it waits in purgatory and what event releases it.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Kafka brokers are often described as 'dumb' compared to RabbitMQ. Why is that a strength?" *Hint: list what the broker does *not* do per message and what the clients take on instead.*

#### Cluster Topology

**Theory**

One broker is a single point of failure with a fixed capacity ceiling. A **Kafka cluster** is a group of nodes that share one set of topics and one consistent view of metadata. Data is spread across brokers for capacity, and copied across brokers for fault tolerance.

In KRaft mode (the only mode in Kafka 4.x), each node has one or both of two **roles**, set by `process.roles`:

| Role | Responsibilities | Typical Count |
|---|---|---|
| `broker` | Stores data, serves clients, replicates partitions | 3 to hundreds |
| `controller` | Stores and manages cluster metadata via a Raft quorum (Section 2.3); elects partition leaders | 3 or 5 |
| `broker,controller` (combined) | Both, in one JVM | Development and very small clusters only |

**Two deployment shapes**

```text
COMBINED MODE (dev / small)                 ISOLATED MODE (production)

+-------------+ +-------------+ +-------------+      +--------+ +--------+ +--------+
| node 1      | | node 2      | | node 3      |      | ctrl 1 | | ctrl 2 | | ctrl 3 |   controller
| broker +    | | broker +    | | broker +    |      | (voter)| | (voter)| | (voter)|   quorum
| controller  | | controller  | | controller  |      +--------+ +--------+ +--------+
+-------------+ +-------------+ +-------------+           |   metadata   |
                                                          v              v
                                             +--------+ +--------+ +--------+ +--------+
 Simple, fewer machines, but a busy          |broker 4| |broker 5| |broker 6| |broker 7|  data
 broker can starve the controller, and       +--------+ +--------+ +--------+ +--------+  plane
 controllers cannot be scaled or                ^           ^           ^          ^
 restarted independently                        +------ producers / consumers -----+
```

Isolated mode is recommended for production because controllers are latency-sensitive: a broker under heavy load (long GC pauses, saturated disks) could otherwise delay metadata operations for the whole cluster. Controller nodes need little disk and modest CPU, so they can be small machines.

**How load is spread**

- **Partitions** of every topic are distributed across brokers.
- **Leadership** is distributed too. Each partition has a **preferred leader** (the first replica in its assignment list), and the controller periodically moves leadership back to preferred leaders (`auto.leader.rebalance.enable=true`) so that one broker does not end up leading everything after a failure.
- Kafka does **not** automatically move partition data when you add a broker. A new broker starts empty until you run a partition reassignment or use a balancing tool such as Cruise Control (Chapter 12).

```text
Topic "orders": 6 partitions, replication factor 3, on 4 brokers  (L = leader, f = follower)

          Broker 1     Broker 2     Broker 3     Broker 4
   P0       L            f            f
   P1                    L            f            f
   P2       f                         L            f
   P3       f            f                         L
   P4       L                         f            f
   P5       f            L            f

   Leaders per broker: B1=2, B2=2, B3=1, B4=1   ->  balanced enough
```

**Cluster identity**

Every cluster has a **cluster ID** (a base64 UUID) generated once and written into each node's storage directory when it is formatted. A node refuses to join a cluster whose ID differs from the one on its disk, which protects against accidentally pointing a broker at the wrong cluster.

**Sizing rules of thumb**

| Question | Rule of Thumb |
|---|---|
| Minimum brokers for production | 3, so that replication factor 3 is possible and one broker can be lost |
| Controllers | 3 (tolerates 1 failure) or 5 (tolerates 2). Never an even number (Section 2.3). |
| When to add brokers | Disk, network, or CPU consistently near capacity; partition counts per broker too high |
| Failure domains | Spread brokers and controllers across racks or availability zones (see Rack Awareness) |

Chapter 13 covers capacity planning in detail.

**Example: inspecting a cluster's topology**

```bash
# Which brokers exist and which API versions they support
bin/kafka-broker-api-versions.sh --bootstrap-server broker4:9092 | grep -E '^[^ ]'

# Where every replica and leader lives for a topic
bin/kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server broker4:9092 --describe --topic orders
```

```text
Topic: orders  TopicId: q8bGv1TfRXSX0n3b1n7Y2w  PartitionCount: 6  ReplicationFactor: 3  Configs: min.insync.replicas=2
    Topic: orders  Partition: 0  Leader: 1  Replicas: 1,2,3  Isr: 1,2,3
    Topic: orders  Partition: 1  Leader: 2  Replicas: 2,3,4  Isr: 2,3,4
    Topic: orders  Partition: 2  Leader: 3  Replicas: 3,4,1  Isr: 3,4,1
    ...
```

(Output abridged.) `Replicas` is the assignment, in order, so its first entry is the preferred leader. `Isr` is explained in Section 2.4.

**Key Takeaways**

- A cluster is a set of nodes sharing topics and metadata. Each node has the `broker` role, the `controller` role, or both.
- Use isolated mode (dedicated controllers) in production. Combined mode is for development and small setups.
- Partitions and their leaders are spread across brokers. Preferred leader election keeps leadership balanced.
- Adding a broker does not move existing data. You must reassign partitions.
- Use at least 3 brokers and an odd number of controllers (3 or 5), spread across failure domains.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. (Beginner) Explain the difference between `process.roles=broker`, `process.roles=controller`, and `process.roles=broker,controller`, and say where each would be used.
> 2. (Intermediate) A cluster has 3 brokers and you add a fourth. A week later, the new broker has almost no disk usage. Explain why, and outline what you would do about it.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Why do production KRaft clusters usually run controllers on separate nodes from brokers?" *Hint: think about what happens to metadata operations, such as leader elections, when the node hosting the active controller is overloaded with client traffic.*

#### Controller Broker

**Theory**

A cluster needs one place where decisions about the whole cluster are made. Who leads partition 7 now that broker 3 has died? Is broker 5 alive? Where should the replicas of a new topic go? If every broker made these decisions on its own, they would disagree. Kafka solves this by having exactly one **active controller** at any time.

> Analogy: the controller is like an air traffic control tower. Planes (brokers) fly on their own and carry the passengers (data), but the tower alone decides who uses which runway (who leads which partition). If the tower goes dark, a standby tower must take over immediately, and planes must never take instructions from two towers at once.

**What the active controller does**

| Task | Description |
|---|---|
| Broker liveness | Tracks broker registrations and heartbeats. Fences brokers that stop heartbeating. |
| Leader election | Chooses new partition leaders when a leader fails, shuts down, or must move (Section 2.4) |
| ISR updates | Accepts and commits changes to in-sync replica sets requested by partition leaders |
| Topic lifecycle | Creates and deletes topics, assigns replicas to brokers, adds partitions |
| Reassignment | Coordinates moving replicas between brokers |
| Configuration, ACLs, quotas, features | Stores and propagates dynamic configuration and security metadata |

The controller is **not** in the data path. Producers and consumers never send records to it. It manages metadata only, which is why a small controller quorum can manage a large cluster.

**The controller over time**

| Aspect | ZooKeeper Era (before 4.0) | KRaft Era (3.3+ and the only option in 4.x) |
|---|---|---|
| Who is controller | One regular broker that won a race to create the `/controller` znode | The leader of the Raft quorum of controller nodes |
| Where metadata lives | ZooKeeper, with a cache in the controller's memory | A replicated metadata log (`__cluster_metadata`) on the controllers |
| Failover | New controller must read **all** metadata from ZooKeeper before acting (seconds to minutes on large clusters) | Standby controllers already hold the metadata log in memory, so failover takes about the election time |
| Pushing changes to brokers | Controller sends RPCs (`LeaderAndIsr`, `UpdateMetadata`) to each broker | Brokers pull the metadata log and apply changes incrementally |
| Fencing a stale controller | `controller epoch` stored in ZooKeeper | Raft leader epoch |

**Fencing: preventing two controllers**

A controller can pause (for example, during a long GC pause), lose its role, and then wake up still believing it is in charge: a **zombie controller**. Kafka prevents its decisions from taking effect with a monotonically increasing **epoch**. Every new controller term has a higher epoch, and requests stamped with an older epoch are rejected. The same idea appears again with leader epochs (Section 2.4) and producer epochs (Chapter 8).

**Broker heartbeats and fencing (KRaft)**

Each broker registers with the controller at startup and then sends a heartbeat every `broker.heartbeat.interval.ms` (default 2 seconds). If no heartbeat arrives within `broker.session.timeout.ms` (default 9 seconds), the controller **fences** the broker: it removes the broker from ISRs and moves leadership of its partitions elsewhere. A fenced broker must catch up on metadata before it is unfenced and allowed to lead again.

```text
broker 3            active controller (ctrl 1)                metadata log
   |  heartbeat (t=0s)     |                                       |
   |---------------------->|                                       |
   |  heartbeat (t=2s)     |                                       |
   |---------------------->|                                       |
   X  broker 3 crashes     |                                       |
                           |  no heartbeat for 9s                  |
                           |-- FenceBrokerRecord(3) -------------->|
                           |-- PartitionChangeRecord(P0: leader 1->2, ISR [2,1]) ->|
                           |                                       |
              all brokers fetch the metadata log and learn the new leaders
```

**Monitoring the controller**

- `kafka.controller:type=KafkaController,name=ActiveControllerCount`: summed across the cluster, this must be exactly **1**. Zero means no controller (metadata changes stall). More than one indicates a serious problem.
- `kafka.controller:type=KafkaController,name=OfflinePartitionsCount`: partitions with no leader. Should be 0.
- Controller event queue time and metadata error rates (Chapter 12).

**Example: finding the active controller**

```bash
bin/kafka-metadata-quorum.sh --bootstrap-server broker4:9092 describe --status
```

```text
ClusterId:              MkU3OEVBNTcwNTJENDM2Qk
LeaderId:               1
LeaderEpoch:            14
HighWatermark:          1873406
MaxFollowerLag:         0
MaxFollowerLagTimeMs:   0
CurrentVoters:          [1,2,3]
CurrentObservers:       [4,5,6,7]
```

(Output abridged; recent versions also print endpoints and directory IDs.) `LeaderId` is the active controller, `LeaderEpoch` increases on every controller change, `CurrentVoters` are the controllers, and `CurrentObservers` are the brokers that replicate the metadata log without voting.

In KRaft clients cannot reach the controllers directly, so the "controller" a client sees in a `Metadata` response is a randomly chosen live broker, which forwards admin requests to the real controller. Do not use a client's reported controller ID to find the active controller. Use the quorum tool or the `ActiveControllerCount` metric instead.

**Key Takeaways**

- Exactly one active controller manages cluster metadata: broker liveness, leader election, ISR changes, topics, configurations, and reassignments.
- The controller is not in the data path. Clients send records to partition leaders, not to the controller.
- In KRaft the active controller is the Raft leader. Standbys already hold the metadata, so failover is fast.
- Epochs fence zombie controllers. Heartbeats and session timeouts fence dead or stuck brokers.
- Watch `ActiveControllerCount` (must sum to 1) and `OfflinePartitionsCount` (must be 0).

> **Practice**
>
> 1. (Beginner) Name three actions that only the active controller performs and one action it never performs.
> 2. (Intermediate) In ZooKeeper mode, controller failover on a cluster with 200,000 partitions could take minutes. Explain what the new controller had to do during that time and why KRaft avoids this.
> 3. **Interview question:** "What is a zombie controller, and how does Kafka stop it from corrupting cluster state?" *Hint: think about a monotonically increasing number attached to every decision.*

#### Broker Discovery and Bootstrap Servers

**Theory**

A client needs to send each record to the leader of its partition, and leaders move around. Hard-coding every broker's address would break whenever the cluster changes. Instead, a client is given a few **bootstrap servers** to start from and discovers the rest of the cluster by asking for **metadata**.

> Analogy: arriving at a large office building, you do not need a directory of every employee's desk. You ask the receptionist (any bootstrap server), who hands you a floor map (metadata) showing where everyone sits. If someone changes desks, you ask again.

**The discovery flow**

```text
 Client                         bootstrap broker (any)                 partition leaders
   |                                    |                                      |
   | 1. TCP connect to one entry in     |                                      |
   |    bootstrap.servers               |                                      |
   |----------------------------------->|                                      |
   | 2. MetadataRequest(topics=[orders])|                                      |
   |----------------------------------->|                                      |
   | 3. MetadataResponse:               |                                      |
   |    brokers = {1: b1:9092, 2: b2:9092, 3: b3:9092}                         |
   |    orders-0 leader=1, orders-1 leader=2, orders-2 leader=3                |
   |<-----------------------------------|                                      |
   | 4. Produce/Fetch go DIRECTLY to each partition's leader                   |
   |-------------------------------------------------------------------------->|
   | 5. On NOT_LEADER_OR_FOLLOWER (leader moved) or every metadata.max.age.ms: |
   |    refresh metadata and retry                                             |
```

Key points:

- **Any** broker can answer a metadata request, because every broker holds a copy of cluster metadata.
- The bootstrap list is only for the **first** contact. After that, the client uses the addresses returned in metadata.
- List **several** bootstrap servers (two or three is enough). If you list just one and it is down when the application starts, the client cannot connect at all. If the list is a single DNS name that resolves to several brokers, the default `client.dns.lookup=use_all_dns_ips` tries each address.
- Clients refresh metadata periodically (`metadata.max.age.ms`, default 5 minutes) and immediately when a request fails with a leadership error.
- Recent clients (3.8+) can re-run the bootstrap step if every known broker becomes unreachable (`metadata.recovery.strategy=rebootstrap`), which helps when an entire cluster is replaced behind the same DNS name.

**The advertised listener trap**

The addresses in the metadata response come from each broker's `advertised.listeners`, **not** from the address the client used to connect. This is the single most common Kafka connectivity problem:

```text
Client on a laptop                       Broker in Docker
bootstrap.servers=localhost:9092  --->   listens on 0.0.0.0:9092
                                         advertised.listeners=PLAINTEXT://kafka:9092
                                  <---   Metadata: "broker 1 is at kafka:9092"
connect to kafka:9092 ... FAILS          (hostname "kafka" only resolves inside Docker)
```

The bootstrap connection succeeds, but every produce or fetch fails or hangs because the client cannot resolve or reach the advertised address. The fix is to advertise an address the client can actually reach, often by using separate listeners for internal and external clients:

```properties
# Broker inside Docker, reachable both from other containers and from the host
listeners=INTERNAL://0.0.0.0:29092,EXTERNAL://0.0.0.0:9092,CONTROLLER://0.0.0.0:9093
advertised.listeners=INTERNAL://kafka:29092,EXTERNAL://localhost:9092
listener.security.protocol.map=INTERNAL:PLAINTEXT,EXTERNAL:PLAINTEXT,CONTROLLER:PLAINTEXT
inter.broker.listener.name=INTERNAL
controller.listener.names=CONTROLLER
# Containers use kafka:29092; applications on the host use localhost:9092
```

**Example: seeing what a client discovers**

```python
from confluent_kafka.admin import AdminClient

admin = AdminClient({"bootstrap.servers": "broker1:9092,broker2:9092,broker3:9092"})
md = admin.list_topics(timeout=10)          # sends a MetadataRequest to one bootstrap server

print("cluster id:", md.cluster_id)
for b in sorted(md.brokers.values(), key=lambda b: b.id):
    # These are the ADVERTISED addresses the client will actually connect to
    print(f"broker {b.id}: {b.host}:{b.port}")

for p in sorted(md.topics["orders"].partitions.values(), key=lambda p: p.id):
    print(f"orders-{p.id}: leader={p.leader} replicas={p.replicas} isr={p.isrs}")
```

```text
cluster id: MkU3OEVBNTcwNTJENDM2Qk
broker 1: broker1.kafka.internal:9092
broker 2: broker2.kafka.internal:9092
broker 3: broker3.kafka.internal:9092
orders-0: leader=1 replicas=[1, 2, 3] isr=[1, 2, 3]
orders-1: leader=2 replicas=[2, 3, 1] isr=[2, 3, 1]
orders-2: leader=3 replicas=[3, 1, 2] isr=[3, 1, 2]
```

If the printed host names are not reachable from where the client runs, you have found an `advertised.listeners` problem.

**Key Takeaways**

- `bootstrap.servers` is only for the first connection. The client learns the full cluster layout from metadata.
- Any broker can answer metadata requests. List two or three bootstrap servers for resilience.
- Clients connect directly to partition leaders and refresh metadata when leadership changes.
- Clients connect to the addresses in `advertised.listeners`. Misconfigured advertised addresses are the most common cause of "connects but cannot produce" problems.
- Use separate listeners for networks that need different addresses (inside Docker or Kubernetes versus outside).

> **Practice**
>
> 1. (Beginner) A cluster has 12 brokers. Does the client's `bootstrap.servers` need to list all 12? Explain what happens if it lists only one and that broker is down at startup.
> 2. (Intermediate) A Kubernetes-hosted broker advertises `kafka-0.kafka-headless.default.svc:9092`. An application outside the cluster can bootstrap through a load balancer but every produce times out. Explain why and sketch a listener configuration that fixes it.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Walk me through what a Kafka producer does between `new KafkaProducer(props)` and the first record landing on the right broker." *Hint: bootstrap, metadata request, partitioner, leader lookup, direct connection, and what triggers a metadata refresh.*

#### Rack Awareness

**Theory**

Replication protects you from losing a broker, but only if the replicas are not all in the same place. If all three replicas of a partition sit in one rack, one top-of-rack switch failure or one power outage takes all of them down at once. **Rack awareness** tells Kafka which failure domain each broker belongs to, so it can spread replicas across them. In the cloud, a "rack" is usually an **availability zone (AZ)**.

> Analogy: you would not keep your house keys, the spare set, and the neighbor's copy all in the same coat pocket. Rack awareness makes sure the copies are in different pockets.

**Configuring racks**

Set `broker.rack` on every broker:

```properties
# Brokers 1 and 4
broker.rack=eu-west-1a
# Brokers 2 and 5
broker.rack=eu-west-1b
# Brokers 3 and 6
broker.rack=eu-west-1c
```

When topics are created or partitions are added, the replica assignment algorithm places each partition's replicas in as many different racks as possible:

```text
              AZ eu-west-1a         AZ eu-west-1b         AZ eu-west-1c
            +---------------+     +---------------+     +---------------+
            | B1      B4    |     | B2      B5    |     | B3      B6    |
   P0       | L             |     | f             |     |         f     |
   P1       |         f     |     |         L     |     | f             |
   P2       | f             |     |         f     |     |         L     |
            +---------------+     +---------------+     +---------------+

   Every partition has exactly one replica per AZ: losing a whole AZ leaves 2 of 3 replicas.
```

Rack-aware placement applies when replicas are **assigned** (topic creation, adding partitions, reassignment). Setting `broker.rack` on an existing cluster does not move existing replicas, so you must reassign them. Keep the number of brokers per rack equal: with uneven racks, the brokers in the smaller rack end up hosting more replicas than the others.

**Follower fetching: reading from the closest replica (KIP-392)**

By default, consumers fetch from the partition leader, which may be in another AZ. Cloud providers charge for cross-AZ traffic, and for a high-throughput topic with many consumer groups this can become a large part of the bill. Since Kafka 2.4, consumers can read from a follower in their own rack:

```properties
# On every broker
replica.selector.class=org.apache.kafka.common.replica.RackAwareReplicaSelector
```

```properties
# On each consumer: the AZ the consumer runs in
client.rack=eu-west-1b
```

```text
Without follower fetching                        With follower fetching

consumer (1b) --cross-AZ--> leader (1a)           consumer (1b) --same AZ--> follower (1b)
                                                   (leader still handles all writes)
```

Trade-offs of follower fetching:

| Benefit | Cost |
|---|---|
| Lower cross-AZ network cost | Slightly higher end-to-end latency: followers only expose data once the high watermark advances, and they learn the new high watermark one fetch later |
| Load spread across more brokers | Requires accurate `client.rack` on every consumer (often injected from cloud instance metadata) |

Consumer groups can also take racks into account when assigning partitions, so that consumers get partitions with a replica in their own rack (KIP-881). Producers always write to the leader, so rack awareness does not reduce produce-side cross-AZ traffic.

**Controllers and racks**

Spread the controller quorum across failure domains too: with 3 controllers in 3 AZs, losing one AZ leaves a 2-of-3 majority. Putting 2 of 3 controllers in the same AZ means losing that AZ stops metadata operations.

**Example: verifying rack placement**

```java
try (Admin admin = Admin.create(Map.of("bootstrap.servers", "broker1:9092"))) {
    // Map broker id -> rack
    Map<Integer, String> rackOf = admin.describeCluster().nodes().get().stream()
        .collect(Collectors.toMap(Node::id, n -> n.hasRack() ? n.rack() : "none"));

    TopicDescription d = admin.describeTopics(List.of("orders")).allTopicNames().get().get("orders");
    for (TopicPartitionInfo p : d.partitions()) {
        Set<String> racks = p.replicas().stream().map(n -> rackOf.get(n.id())).collect(Collectors.toSet());
        boolean ok = racks.size() == p.replicas().size();   // one replica per distinct rack?
        System.out.printf("orders-%d replicas=%s racks=%s %s%n",
            p.partition(), p.replicas().stream().map(Node::id).toList(), racks, ok ? "OK" : "SHARED RACK");
    }
}
```

**Key Takeaways**

- `broker.rack` tells Kafka each broker's failure domain (rack or AZ), so it spreads a partition's replicas across domains.
- Placement is applied when replicas are assigned. Existing topics need reassignment after racks are added or changed.
- Keep brokers balanced across racks to avoid hot spots.
- Follower fetching (`RackAwareReplicaSelector` + `client.rack`) lets consumers read from a same-AZ replica, which cuts cross-AZ costs at a small latency cost.
- Spread controllers across failure domains so that losing one domain does not cost the quorum its majority.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. (Beginner) A cluster has 6 brokers in 3 AZs and topics use replication factor 3. How many AZs can fail before a partition loses all its replicas, assuming rack-aware placement?
> 2. (Intermediate) A topic produces 50 MB/s and is read by 4 consumer groups, with consumers evenly spread across 3 AZs. Estimate the cross-AZ consumer traffic per second with and without follower fetching. (Assume leaders are evenly spread across AZs.)
> 3. **Interview question:** "Your cloud bill shows very high inter-AZ data transfer from Kafka. What would you investigate and change?" *Hint: separate replication traffic (unavoidable with replicas in different AZs) from consumer and producer traffic, and consider which of them can be kept local.*

<a id="23-cluster-metadata-management"></a>
### 2.3 Cluster Metadata Management

Every broker must agree on which topics exist, where their replicas live, who leads each partition, and which brokers are alive. This section explains how Kafka stores and agrees on that metadata, first with ZooKeeper and now with KRaft, and how existing clusters move from one to the other.

#### ZooKeeper-Based Architecture

**Theory**

From its first release until version 3.x, Kafka did not store its own metadata. It delegated that job to **Apache ZooKeeper**, a separate distributed coordination service that offers a small, strongly consistent, tree-shaped key-value store. Kafka 4.0 (March 2025) removed ZooKeeper support entirely, but you still need to understand the old design: many production clusters ran on it for years, much of Kafka's documentation and tooling history refers to it, and migrating off it is a real operational task (see Migrating from ZooKeeper to KRaft).

> Analogy: ZooKeeper was like an external notary office. Kafka brokers did their own work, but every important fact (who is alive, who leads what) had to be registered with the notary, and the notary's records were the official truth.

**What ZooKeeper provided**

ZooKeeper stores data in **znodes** arranged like a file system. Two features made it useful for Kafka:

- **Ephemeral znodes**: they exist only while the session that created them is alive. A broker that crashes loses its session, so its znode disappears automatically. This gave Kafka failure detection.
- **Watches**: a client can ask to be notified when a znode changes. The controller watched broker registrations and admin requests.

```text
ZooKeeper tree used by Kafka (under an optional chroot such as /kafka)

/
|-- cluster/id                        cluster ID
|-- controller                        EPHEMERAL: {"brokerid":1}  <- whoever creates it first is controller
|-- controller_epoch                  17                          <- fencing for zombie controllers
|-- brokers/
|   |-- ids/1, ids/2, ids/3           EPHEMERAL: one per live broker (host, ports, rack)
|   `-- topics/orders                 replica assignment {"0":[1,2,3],"1":[2,3,1],...}
|        `-- partitions/0/state       {"leader":1,"leader_epoch":5,"isr":[1,2,3]}
|-- config/
|   |-- topics/orders                 topic-level config overrides
|   `-- brokers/, users/, clients/    dynamic broker configs, quotas
|-- admin/
|   |-- delete_topics/                pending topic deletions
|   `-- reassign_partitions           in-progress reassignment
`-- kafka-acl/                        ACLs (ZooKeeper-based authorizer)
```

**How the pieces worked together**

1. Each broker, on startup, created an ephemeral znode under `/brokers/ids/`.
2. All brokers raced to create the ephemeral `/controller` znode. The winner became the **controller**. The others set a watch on it, so they could race again if it disappeared.
3. The controller watched `/brokers/ids`. When a broker's znode disappeared, the controller chose new leaders for that broker's partitions, wrote the new state to ZooKeeper, and then sent `LeaderAndIsr` and `UpdateMetadata` RPCs to every affected broker.
4. Partition leaders wrote ISR changes directly to ZooKeeper, and the controller propagated them.

```text
                +-------------------------------+
                |     ZooKeeper ensemble        |
                |   zk1      zk2      zk3       |   source of truth for metadata
                +-------------------------------+
                  ^  watches / writes      ^ ephemeral registrations, ISR writes
                  |                        |
          +--------------+        +--------------+  +--------------+
          |  Broker 1    |        |  Broker 2    |  |  Broker 3    |
          | (CONTROLLER) |------->|              |  |              |
          +--------------+  RPCs  +--------------+  +--------------+
                  |       LeaderAndIsr, UpdateMetadata        ^
                  +-------------------------------------------+
```

**Why Kafka moved away from ZooKeeper**

| Problem | Explanation |
|---|---|
| Two distributed systems to run | Separate deployment, configuration, security (SASL, TLS, ACLs), monitoring, and upgrades for ZooKeeper |
| Slow controller failover | A new controller had to read the full state of every partition from ZooKeeper before acting. On large clusters this took tens of seconds to minutes, during which leader elections stalled. |
| Scalability ceiling | Metadata had to fit ZooKeeper's model and the controller's reload time. Practical limits were around 200,000 partitions per cluster. |
| Divergent views | Metadata lived in ZooKeeper, in the controller's memory, and in each broker's cache, updated by separate RPCs. These copies could drift apart, causing subtle bugs. |
| Inefficient propagation | Changes were pushed to brokers as full or partial snapshots, not as an ordered log of deltas. |

The insight behind the replacement (KIP-500) was: Kafka is already a replicated log system, so it should store its own metadata in a replicated log.

**Example: what operating a ZooKeeper-based cluster looked like (historical, 3.x and earlier)**

```properties
# server.properties of a ZooKeeper-mode broker
broker.id=1
zookeeper.connect=zk1:2181,zk2:2181,zk3:2181/kafka   # "/kafka" is a chroot path
zookeeper.session.timeout.ms=18000
listeners=PLAINTEXT://0.0.0.0:9092
log.dirs=/var/lib/kafka/data
```

```bash
# Inspecting cluster state directly in ZooKeeper
bin/zookeeper-shell.sh zk1:2181/kafka get /controller
# {"version":2,"brokerid":1,"timestamp":"1761210942120"}

bin/zookeeper-shell.sh zk1:2181/kafka ls /brokers/ids
# [1, 2, 3]

bin/zookeeper-shell.sh zk1:2181/kafka get /brokers/topics/orders/partitions/0/state
# {"controller_epoch":17,"leader":1,"version":1,"leader_epoch":5,"isr":[1,2,3]}
```

Older CLI tools even accepted `--zookeeper` instead of `--bootstrap-server`, letting them bypass the brokers. Those options were removed during the 3.x line, and none of this works in Kafka 4.x.

**Key Takeaways**

- Up to Kafka 3.x, ZooKeeper held all cluster metadata. Kafka 4.0 removed ZooKeeper support.
- Ephemeral znodes detected broker failures. A race on the `/controller` znode chose the controller.
- The controller read state from ZooKeeper and pushed changes to brokers with RPCs.
- Its main problems were operational complexity, slow controller failover, limited partition scalability, and inconsistent copies of metadata.
- KRaft replaced it by storing metadata in a Kafka-native replicated log.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. (Beginner) Explain how ZooKeeper's ephemeral znodes allowed Kafka to detect a crashed broker.
> 2. (Intermediate) Describe the sequence of events, from broker crash to clients producing again, in ZooKeeper mode. Identify the step that grew slower as the number of partitions grew.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Why did Kafka remove its dependency on ZooKeeper?" *Hint: give at least one operational reason, one performance reason, and one correctness reason.*

#### KRaft Mode

**Theory**

**KRaft** (Kafka Raft, introduced by KIP-500) moves metadata management inside Kafka. A small set of **controller** nodes form a **Raft quorum** and store every metadata change as a record in an internal, single-partition log called `__cluster_metadata`. The leader of that quorum is the **active controller**. Brokers replicate this log too, and build their view of the cluster by applying its records in order.

> Analogy: instead of registering facts with an outside notary (ZooKeeper), the company now keeps its own official ledger, maintained by a small board (the controllers). Every branch office (broker) keeps a copy of the ledger and stays current by reading new entries as they are written.

**Milestones**

| Version | Date | Milestone |
|---|---|---|
| 2.8 | April 2021 | KRaft available as early access |
| 3.3 | October 2022 | KRaft production-ready for new clusters |
| 3.4 | February 2023 | ZooKeeper-to-KRaft migration available as early access |
| 3.5 | June 2023 | ZooKeeper mode deprecated |
| 3.6 | October 2023 | Migration production-ready |
| 3.9 | November 2024 | Last 3.x release and the final "bridge" release for migration. Dynamic controller quorums (KIP-853). |
| 4.0 | March 2025 | ZooKeeper removed. KRaft is the only mode. |

**Metadata as an event log**

Every change to the cluster is a typed record appended to `__cluster_metadata`:

| Record Type | Written When |
|---|---|
| `RegisterBrokerRecord` | A broker starts and registers |
| `FenceBrokerRecord` / `UnfenceBrokerRecord` | A broker stops heartbeating, or catches up and becomes eligible |
| `TopicRecord` | A topic is created |
| `PartitionRecord` | A partition is created (replicas, leader, ISR) |
| `PartitionChangeRecord` | Leader, ISR, or replicas of a partition change |
| `ConfigRecord` | A dynamic configuration is set |
| `FeatureLevelRecord` | A feature such as `metadata.version` is upgraded |
| `RemoveTopicRecord` | A topic is deleted |

This is the same idea as event sourcing (Chapter 15): the current metadata is the result of replaying the log. Instead of pushing state with RPCs, the controller just appends records, and every broker **pulls** new records with `Fetch` requests, like a consumer. Consequences:

- **Consistency**: every node applies the same records in the same order, so all views converge. A broker knows exactly how up to date it is (by metadata offset).
- **Fast failover**: standby controllers are already replicating the log and hold the full metadata in memory. A new active controller can act as soon as it is elected.
- **Incremental propagation**: brokers receive small deltas instead of full state snapshots.
- **Scale**: metadata operations no longer slow down proportionally to the total partition count, which raises practical cluster limits to millions of partitions.

```text
          Controller quorum (voters)                   Brokers (observers)
   +-----------+  +-----------+  +-----------+
   | ctrl 1    |  | ctrl 2    |  | ctrl 3    |        +----------+  +----------+
   | ACTIVE    |  | standby   |  | standby   |        | broker 4 |  | broker 5 |
   | (leader)  |  | (follower)|  | (follower)|        |          |  |          |
   +-----------+  +-----------+  +-----------+        +----------+  +----------+
        |  __cluster_metadata (single partition)            ^             ^
        |  offset ... 812 813 814 815                       |   Fetch     |
        +---> followers Fetch from the leader               +-------------+
                                                       brokers Fetch the same log and
                                                       apply records to an in-memory cache
```

**Snapshots**

An ever-growing metadata log would make restarts slow. Controllers and brokers therefore write **snapshots** of their in-memory metadata periodically (controlled by `metadata.log.max.record.bytes.between.snapshots` and `metadata.log.max.snapshot.interval.ms`). A restarting node loads the latest snapshot and replays only the records after it. A node that has fallen too far behind downloads the snapshot from the leader.

**Feature versioning**

A KRaft cluster tracks a **`metadata.version`** feature level, which controls the metadata record formats and protocol features in use. After upgrading the software on every node, you upgrade the feature level explicitly:

```bash
bin/kafka-features.sh --bootstrap-server broker4:9092 describe
bin/kafka-features.sh --bootstrap-server broker4:9092 upgrade --release-version 4.1
```

This replaces the older `inter.broker.protocol.version` setting from ZooKeeper mode and lets you finish a rolling upgrade before turning on new features.

**Example: starting a KRaft cluster**

Single-node development setup (combined mode, as in the official quickstart):

```bash
# 1. Generate a cluster ID once
KAFKA_CLUSTER_ID="$(bin/kafka-storage.sh random-uuid)"

# 2. Format the storage directory: writes meta.properties (cluster ID, node ID)
#    and bootstraps a one-voter controller quorum
bin/kafka-storage.sh format --standalone -t "$KAFKA_CLUSTER_ID" -c config/server.properties

# 3. Start the node (process.roles=broker,controller in this file)
bin/kafka-server-start.sh config/server.properties
```

Production setup (isolated mode, static quorum shown for clarity):

```properties
# controller.properties  (on ctrl1; ctrl2 and ctrl3 differ only in node.id and listener host)
process.roles=controller
node.id=1
controller.quorum.voters=1@ctrl1:9093,2@ctrl2:9093,3@ctrl3:9093   # fixed voter set
listeners=CONTROLLER://ctrl1:9093
controller.listener.names=CONTROLLER
listener.security.protocol.map=CONTROLLER:PLAINTEXT
log.dirs=/var/lib/kafka/meta                                    # holds __cluster_metadata
```

```properties
# broker.properties  (on broker4)
process.roles=broker
node.id=4                                                        # must not clash with controller IDs
controller.quorum.voters=1@ctrl1:9093,2@ctrl2:9093,3@ctrl3:9093
controller.listener.names=CONTROLLER
listeners=PLAINTEXT://broker4:9092
listener.security.protocol.map=PLAINTEXT:PLAINTEXT,CONTROLLER:PLAINTEXT
log.dirs=/var/lib/kafka/data
```

```bash
# Every node (controllers and brokers) is formatted with the SAME cluster ID
bin/kafka-storage.sh format -t "$KAFKA_CLUSTER_ID" -c controller.properties   # on each controller
bin/kafka-storage.sh format -t "$KAFKA_CLUSTER_ID" -c broker.properties       # on each broker
```

With a **dynamic quorum** (3.9+), you instead set `controller.quorum.bootstrap.servers` and format the controllers with `--initial-controllers` (or `--standalone` for the first one), which allows adding and removing controllers later (see Metadata Quorum and Raft Consensus).

Inspecting the metadata log directly:

```bash
bin/kafka-dump-log.sh --cluster-metadata-decoder \
  --files /var/lib/kafka/meta/__cluster_metadata-0/00000000000000000000.log
```

```text
| offset: 812 ... payload: {"type":"TOPIC_RECORD","version":0,"data":{"name":"orders","topicId":"q8bGv1TfRXSX0n3b1n7Y2w"}}
| offset: 813 ... payload: {"type":"PARTITION_RECORD","version":0,"data":{"partitionId":0,"topicId":"q8bG...","replicas":[4,5,6],"isr":[4,5,6],"leader":4,"leaderEpoch":0}}
| offset: 940 ... payload: {"type":"PARTITION_CHANGE_RECORD","version":0,"data":{"partitionId":0,"topicId":"q8bG...","isr":[5,6],"leader":5}}
```

(Output abridged.) Offset 940 records broker 4 losing leadership of `orders-0`: a single small delta, not a full state rewrite.

**Key Takeaways**

- KRaft stores cluster metadata in an internal Raft-replicated log, `__cluster_metadata`, managed by controller nodes. The Raft leader is the active controller.
- Brokers replicate the metadata log as observers and apply its records to an in-memory cache, so all nodes converge on the same state.
- Failover is fast because standby controllers already hold the metadata. Propagation is incremental and scales to far more partitions.
- Snapshots bound restart and catch-up time. `metadata.version` gates new features after an upgrade.
- Every node must be formatted with `kafka-storage.sh` using the same cluster ID before first start.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. (Beginner) What is stored in `__cluster_metadata`, and how do brokers keep their copy up to date?
> 2. (Intermediate) Set up a three-node combined-mode KRaft cluster locally (three configuration files, different ports and `node.id`s). Use `kafka-metadata-quorum.sh describe --status` to find the active controller, stop it, and observe the new `LeaderId` and `LeaderEpoch`.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Compare how a leader change is propagated to brokers in ZooKeeper mode and in KRaft mode." *Hint: push RPCs with full or partial state versus pull of an ordered log of deltas; consider what happens to a broker that misses an update in each model.*

#### Metadata Quorum and Raft Consensus

**Theory**

The controllers must agree on a single, ordered metadata log even when some of them crash or the network splits. This is the classic problem of **distributed consensus**. KRaft solves it with a variant of the **Raft** algorithm. You do not need to implement Raft to operate Kafka, but you do need its core ideas to size the quorum and understand failure behavior.

> Analogy: a committee that keeps the official minutes. One member is the chair (leader) and is the only one allowed to write new entries. An entry becomes official once a majority of members have copied it into their own notebooks. If the chair disappears, the members vote for a new chair, and only someone whose notebook is fully up to date can win.

**Raft in five ideas**

1. **Roles**: each voter is a **leader**, a **follower**, or a **candidate**. KRaft adds **observers** (brokers), which replicate the log but never vote.
2. **Epochs (terms)**: time is divided into numbered epochs, each with at most one leader. A higher epoch always wins, which fences old leaders.
3. **Leader election**: if a follower hears nothing from the leader for a while, it becomes a candidate, increments the epoch, and asks for votes. A voter grants its vote only if the candidate's log is at least as up to date as its own. A candidate with votes from a **majority** becomes leader.
4. **Log replication**: only the leader appends. Followers copy its log in order.
5. **Commitment**: an entry is **committed** once a majority of voters have it. Committed entries are never lost, because any future leader must have them (it needed a majority's votes, and any two majorities overlap).

**How KRaft differs from textbook Raft**

| Aspect | Textbook Raft | KRaft |
|---|---|---|
| Replication | Leader **pushes** entries with `AppendEntries` | Followers and observers **pull** with `Fetch`, reusing Kafka's replication machinery |
| Leader liveness | Leader sends heartbeats | Followers' regular fetches double as liveness signals. A follower that cannot fetch within `controller.quorum.fetch.timeout.ms` starts an election. |
| Commit point | Commit index | The metadata log's **high watermark** |
| Non-voting replicas | Learners (an extension) | Observers: every broker |
| Divergent logs | Leader overwrites follower entries | Leader returns a "diverging epoch" in the fetch response, and the follower truncates to the right point |

Newer versions also add a **pre-vote** phase (KIP-996): a node first checks whether it *could* win before starting a real election, which prevents a node with a flaky network link from repeatedly bumping the epoch and disrupting a healthy leader.

**Committing a metadata record**

```text
Voters: ctrl1 (leader), ctrl2, ctrl3          majority = 2

1. Admin creates a topic -> ctrl1 appends TopicRecord at offset 815    ctrl1 LEO=816
2. ctrl2 Fetch(offset=815) -> receives 815                             ctrl2 LEO=816
3. ctrl3 is slow, still at LEO=815
4. ctrl2's next Fetch(offset=816) tells ctrl1 "I have up to 815"
   -> 2 of 3 voters have 815 -> high watermark advances to 816        COMMITTED
5. Only now does ctrl1 answer the CreateTopics request successfully,
   and brokers (observers) apply the record once they see HW >= 816
```

**Sizing the quorum**

| Voters | Majority Needed | Failures Tolerated | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1 | 0 | Development only |
| 2 | 2 | 0 | Worse than 1: two machines that can fail, and no extra tolerance |
| 3 | 2 | 1 | Standard choice |
| 4 | 3 | 1 | No benefit over 3, more replication work |
| 5 | 3 | 2 | Large or critical clusters, or to survive one failure during maintenance |

Use an odd number. Adding an even-numbered voter raises the majority without raising tolerance. More voters also mean every commit waits for more acknowledgments, so 3 or 5 is almost always right.

**What happens when the quorum loses its majority**

If a majority of controllers is unavailable, no new leader can be elected and no metadata record can be committed. Brokers **keep serving reads and writes** for partitions whose leaders are healthy, using their last known metadata, but nothing that needs the controller works: no leader elections after broker failures, no topic creation, no ISR changes, no configuration updates. This is why controllers must be spread across failure domains.

**Dynamic quorum membership (KIP-853, Kafka 3.9+)**

Originally the voter set was fixed by `controller.quorum.voters`, and changing it required downtime. With dynamic quorums, nodes find the quorum through `controller.quorum.bootstrap.servers`, and voters can be added or removed online:

```bash
# On a new, formatted controller that has started and caught up as an observer:
bin/kafka-metadata-quorum.sh --command-config new-controller.properties \
  --bootstrap-controller ctrl1:9093 add-controller

# Remove a voter (identified by node ID and its storage directory ID)
bin/kafka-metadata-quorum.sh --bootstrap-controller ctrl1:9093 \
  remove-controller --controller-id 3 --controller-directory-id <directory-uuid>
```

The directory ID identifies a specific disk, so a controller whose disk was wiped and re-formatted cannot silently rejoin as if it still had its old data, which would be unsafe for Raft.

**Example: observing replication in the quorum**

```bash
bin/kafka-metadata-quorum.sh --bootstrap-server broker4:9092 describe --replication
```

```text
NodeId  LogEndOffset  Lag  LastFetchTimestamp  LastCaughtUpTimestamp  Status
1       1873406       0    1761210942120       1761210942120          Leader
2       1873406       0    1761210942051       1761210942051          Follower
3       1873390       16   1761210941830       1761210941200          Follower
4       1873406       0    1761210942090       1761210942090          Observer
5       1873406       0    1761210942077       1761210942077          Observer
```

(Output abridged.) Node 3 is lagging slightly. If its lag grows steadily, that controller may have disk or network problems.

A small Python model of the commit rule:

```python
def high_watermark(leader_leo: int, follower_leos: list[int]) -> int:
    """The highest offset present on a majority of voters (exclusive end, like Kafka's HW)."""
    leos = sorted([leader_leo, *follower_leos], reverse=True)
    majority = len(leos) // 2 + 1
    return leos[majority - 1]      # the majority-th largest LEO is held by >= majority voters

print(high_watermark(816, [816, 815]))            # 3 voters  -> 816 (ctrl1 and ctrl2 have it)
print(high_watermark(820, [816, 815, 812, 810]))  # 5 voters  -> 815
print(high_watermark(820, [815, 815]))            # leader ahead alone -> 815, not 820
```

**Key Takeaways**

- KRaft controllers run a Raft variant: one leader per epoch, majority-based election and commitment, with followers pulling via `Fetch`.
- A metadata change takes effect only after a majority of voters have it (the high watermark advances).
- Use 3 or 5 voters. An odd number gives the best fault tolerance per node. Spread them across failure domains.
- Without a majority, data traffic on healthy partitions continues, but all metadata changes, including failover, stop.
- Dynamic quorums (3.9+) allow adding and removing controllers online. Directory IDs protect against unsafe rejoining with wiped disks.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. (Beginner) A quorum has 5 voters. How many can fail while the cluster still elects partition leaders? What if it has 4 voters?
> 2. (Intermediate) Two of three controllers are in AZ `a` and one is in AZ `b`. AZ `a` fails. Describe what still works and what stops working for producers, consumers, and administrators. Propose a better placement.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Why can a Raft-based system never lose a committed entry, even if the leader crashes right after committing?" *Hint: combine two facts: an entry is committed on a majority, and a candidate needs votes from a majority whose logs are not more up to date than its own.*

#### Migrating from ZooKeeper to KRaft

**Theory**

Clusters created before KRaft must be moved to it before they can run Kafka 4.x, because 4.0 and later cannot start in ZooKeeper mode or perform the migration. The migration is done **online**, without downtime for clients, using a 3.x **bridge release** (3.9 is the last and recommended one). After migrating on 3.9, you upgrade to 4.x as a normal rolling upgrade.

> Analogy: moving a shop's records from a filing cabinet to a new computer system while the shop stays open. First the new system copies everything from the cabinet. For a while, every change is written to both, so you can still go back. Once everyone uses the new system and you are confident, you stop updating the cabinet and finally remove it.

**Prerequisites**

- All brokers run the bridge release (for example 3.9.x) with `inter.broker.protocol.version` set to that version.
- You know the existing cluster ID (stored in ZooKeeper at `/cluster/id`).
- Your configuration uses only features supported by migration in that release (check the release's migration documentation, for example for JBOD or specific security setups).
- Monitoring is in place for both the old and the new metadata systems, and you have rehearsed in a staging cluster.

**The migration phases**

```text
Phase 0  ZooKeeper mode
         [ZooKeeper] <-> brokers (one broker is the ZK controller)

Phase 1  Deploy KRaft controllers with migration enabled
         [ZooKeeper]     [ctrl quorum: waiting for brokers]
              ^
           brokers (still ZK mode)

Phase 2  Enable migration on brokers (rolling restart, still ZK mode)
         -> a KRaft controller becomes the active controller
         -> it copies all metadata from ZooKeeper into __cluster_metadata
         -> DUAL-WRITE: every metadata change is written to the KRaft log AND to ZooKeeper
         [ZooKeeper] <-dual-write- [ctrl quorum ACTIVE] --RPCs--> brokers (ZK mode)

Phase 3  Restart brokers as KRaft brokers (rolling restart)
         brokers now fetch __cluster_metadata; dual-write to ZooKeeper continues
         [ZooKeeper] <-dual-write- [ctrl quorum] <--Fetch-- brokers (KRaft mode)

Phase 4  Finalize: restart controllers without ZooKeeper configuration
         ZooKeeper no longer updated -> decommission it          POINT OF NO RETURN
         [ctrl quorum] <--Fetch-- brokers (KRaft mode)
```

Until Phase 4, ZooKeeper still receives every metadata change, so you can **roll back** to ZooKeeper mode by following the documented reverse procedure. After finalization, rolling back is no longer possible.

**Monitoring progress**

- The controller logs `Completed migration of metadata from ZooKeeper to KRaft` when the Phase 2 copy finishes.
- The metric `kafka.controller:type=KafkaController,name=ZkMigrationState` shows the current migration state.
- Check that `ActiveControllerCount` is 1 on the KRaft quorum, and that there are no offline or under-replicated partitions after each rolling restart.

**Alternative: migrate by building a new cluster**

Some teams avoid in-place migration altogether: they create a fresh KRaft cluster, replicate topics with MirrorMaker 2 or a similar tool (Chapter 14), move consumers and then producers over, and retire the old cluster. This costs more infrastructure and needs careful offset translation, but it is also a chance to fix old topic layouts and configurations.

| Approach | Advantages | Disadvantages |
|---|---|---|
| In-place migration | No data copying, same endpoints, same offsets, rollback until finalization | Several rolling restarts on a live cluster, must stay on 3.x until done |
| New cluster + replication | Clean slate, can upgrade straight to 4.x | Double infrastructure for a while, client cutover, offset translation |

**Example: configuration in each phase (static quorum, 3.9)**

Phase 1, controller configuration:

```properties
process.roles=controller
node.id=3000                                      # choose IDs that do not clash with broker.ids
controller.quorum.voters=3000@ctrl1:9093,3001@ctrl2:9093,3002@ctrl3:9093
controller.listener.names=CONTROLLER
listeners=CONTROLLER://:9093

# Migration
zookeeper.metadata.migration.enable=true
zookeeper.connect=zk1:2181,zk2:2181,zk3:2181/kafka

# So the controller can send RPCs to brokers that are still in ZooKeeper mode
inter.broker.listener.name=PLAINTEXT
listener.security.protocol.map=PLAINTEXT:PLAINTEXT,CONTROLLER:PLAINTEXT
```

```bash
# Format controllers with the EXISTING cluster ID read from ZooKeeper (/cluster/id)
bin/kafka-storage.sh format -t "<existing-cluster-id>" -c controller.properties
```

Phase 2, broker configuration (still ZooKeeper mode, now aware of the controllers):

```properties
broker.id=0
listeners=PLAINTEXT://:9092
advertised.listeners=PLAINTEXT://broker0:9092
listener.security.protocol.map=PLAINTEXT:PLAINTEXT,CONTROLLER:PLAINTEXT
inter.broker.protocol.version=3.9

zookeeper.connect=zk1:2181,zk2:2181,zk3:2181/kafka
zookeeper.metadata.migration.enable=true          # added
controller.quorum.voters=3000@ctrl1:9093,3001@ctrl2:9093,3002@ctrl3:9093   # added
controller.listener.names=CONTROLLER              # added
```

Phase 3, broker configuration (KRaft mode):

```properties
process.roles=broker                              # added
node.id=0                                         # same value as the old broker.id
listeners=PLAINTEXT://:9092
advertised.listeners=PLAINTEXT://broker0:9092
listener.security.protocol.map=PLAINTEXT:PLAINTEXT,CONTROLLER:PLAINTEXT
controller.quorum.voters=3000@ctrl1:9093,3001@ctrl2:9093,3002@ctrl3:9093
controller.listener.names=CONTROLLER
# removed: broker.id, zookeeper.connect, zookeeper.metadata.migration.enable,
```
