Writing producers and consumers is only half of working with Kafka. The other half is keeping the cluster healthy for months and years: configuring brokers and the machines under them, restarting and upgrading without downtime, moving data as the cluster grows, watching the right signals, and knowing what to do when something breaks at 3 a.m. This chapter covers that operational side in four parts: **cluster configuration**, **cluster maintenance**, **monitoring and observability**, and **troubleshooting**. Most production incidents involving Kafka come from operational gaps (a missing alert, an untested upgrade, a full disk), not from bugs in Kafka itself, so this material matters as much as any API.

<a id="121-cluster-configuration"></a>
### 12.1 Cluster Configuration

This section covers how to configure a production cluster from the broker properties file down to the hardware: which broker settings matter most, how to change settings at runtime, and how to tune the operating system, the JVM, and the disks that Kafka runs on.

#### Broker Configuration Essentials

**Theory**

A Kafka broker has several hundred configuration properties, and almost all of them have reasonable defaults. The problem is that the defaults are tuned for **getting started**, not for production. A broker started from the sample `server.properties` creates topics automatically, keeps one copy of internal data on a single-node cluster, and uses thread pools sized for a laptop. None of this breaks anything on day one, but each default becomes a failure mode later: a typo in a topic name creates a topic nobody intended, a replication factor of 1 turns a disk failure into data loss, and an undersized recovery thread pool turns a routine restart into a 40-minute outage.

> Analogy: the defaults are a rental car's factory settings. The car drives, but before a long trip you adjust the seat, the mirrors, and the tire pressure for your own load. Leaving the defaults unchanged is not wrong. It just means you never decided anything.

It helps to sort broker settings into groups and decide each group deliberately:

| Group | Key settings | What goes wrong if ignored |
|---|---|---|
| Identity and roles | `process.roles`, `node.id`, `broker.rack` | Duplicate IDs prevent startup; no rack means replicas can land in one AZ |
| Controller quorum | `controller.quorum.bootstrap.servers` (or `controller.quorum.voters`), `controller.listener.names` | Broker cannot register with the cluster |
| Networking | `listeners`, `advertised.listeners`, `listener.security.protocol.map`, `inter.broker.listener.name` | Clients connect to unreachable addresses (Section 2.2) |
| Storage | `log.dirs`, `metadata.log.dir` | Data on the OS disk; metadata competing with data I/O |
| Topic defaults | `num.partitions`, `default.replication.factor`, `min.insync.replicas`, `auto.create.topics.enable` | Accidental topics with RF=1 and one partition |
| Internal topics | `offsets.topic.replication.factor`, `transaction.state.log.replication.factor`, `transaction.state.log.min.isr` | Consumer offsets or transactions lost with one broker |
| Retention | `log.retention.hours`/`ms`, `log.retention.bytes`, `log.segment.bytes` | Disks fill up, or data is deleted too early (Section 7.2) |
| Availability vs safety | `unclean.leader.election.enable`, `replica.lag.time.max.ms` | Silent data loss, or flapping ISR (Section 2.4) |
| Limits | `message.max.bytes`, `replica.fetch.max.bytes`, `max.connections.per.ip` | Large records rejected or not replicated; connection floods |
| Threads | `num.network.threads`, `num.io.threads`, `num.replica.fetchers`, `num.recovery.threads.per.data.dir` | Request queuing, slow replication, slow restarts (Chapter 13) |
| Group coordination | `group.initial.rebalance.delay.ms` | Many rebalances when a whole application starts at once |

**Settings that deserve special attention**

- **`auto.create.topics.enable`** (default `true`): any producer or consumer that references a missing topic creates it with the broker defaults. In production, disable it and create topics explicitly (Section 3.3) so partition count, replication factor, and configs are always chosen.
- **`default.replication.factor`** (default `1`) and **`min.insync.replicas`** (default `1`): set them to 3 and 2 so that even topics created without explicit settings survive a broker failure.
- **`offsets.topic.replication.factor`** and **`transaction.state.log.replication.factor`** (default `3`): keep them at 3. They only take effect when the internal topic is first created, so a cluster that was briefly started with one broker and an override of 1 keeps RF=1 for `__consumer_offsets` forever unless you reassign it.
- **`message.max.bytes`** (default about 1 MB): the largest record batch a broker accepts. If you raise it, also raise `max.request.size` on producers (or they reject large records themselves) and keep `replica.fetch.max.bytes` and the consumers' `max.partition.fetch.bytes` aligned with it. Since KIP-74 these fetch limits are soft (an oversized first batch is still returned so fetching makes progress), but mismatched limits make replication and consumption inefficient and confuse whoever reads the configuration later.
- **`num.recovery.threads.per.data.dir`**: threads per log directory used to load and recover segments at startup and flush at shutdown. After an unclean shutdown, a broker with thousands of partitions may take a long time to recover with only a few threads. Values of 4 to 8 per directory are common on machines with fast disks.
- **`broker.rack`**: enables rack-aware replica placement (Section 2.2). Set it to the availability zone in the cloud.

**Example: a production-oriented broker configuration**

```properties
# ===== Identity =====
process.roles=broker
node.id=4
broker.rack=eu-west-1a                          # AZ name; replicas of a partition spread across racks

# ===== Controller quorum =====
controller.quorum.bootstrap.servers=ctrl1:9093,ctrl2:9093,ctrl3:9093
controller.listener.names=CONTROLLER

# ===== Networking =====
listeners=INTERNAL://0.0.0.0:9092,EXTERNAL://0.0.0.0:9094
advertised.listeners=INTERNAL://broker4.kafka.internal:9092,EXTERNAL://kafka4.example.com:9094
listener.security.protocol.map=INTERNAL:SSL,EXTERNAL:SASL_SSL,CONTROLLER:SSL
inter.broker.listener.name=INTERNAL

# ===== Storage: one directory per physical disk =====
log.dirs=/data/kafka-1,/data/kafka-2,/data/kafka-3
num.recovery.threads.per.data.dir=4             # faster startup after a crash

# ===== Safe defaults for topics created without explicit settings =====
auto.create.topics.enable=false
num.partitions=6
default.replication.factor=3
min.insync.replicas=2
unclean.leader.election.enable=false

# ===== Internal topics =====
offsets.topic.replication.factor=3
transaction.state.log.replication.factor=3
transaction.state.log.min.isr=2

# ===== Retention and segments =====
log.retention.hours=168                         # 7 days unless the topic overrides it
log.segment.bytes=1073741824                    # 1 GiB segments (default)
log.retention.check.interval.ms=300000

# ===== Limits =====
message.max.bytes=2097152                       # 2 MiB batches accepted...
replica.fetch.max.bytes=2097152                 # ...and replicated
max.connections.per.ip=500                      # protects against client connection leaks

# ===== Threads (starting points; tune with metrics, Chapter 13) =====
num.network.threads=6
num.io.threads=16
num.replica.fetchers=4
```

**Verifying what a running broker actually uses**

The properties file is only one source of truth. Dynamic overrides (next topic) take precedence, so always check the effective configuration:

```bash
# Every effective value on broker 4, with its source (STATIC_BROKER_CONFIG, DYNAMIC_BROKER_CONFIG, DEFAULT_CONFIG, ...)
bin/kafka-configs.sh --bootstrap-server broker4.kafka.internal:9092 \
  --describe --broker 4 --all | grep -E 'min.insync|replication.factor|auto.create'
```

**Key Takeaways**

- The defaults make getting started easy. They are not production settings. Decide each group of settings deliberately.
- Disable `auto.create.topics.enable` and set `default.replication.factor=3` and `min.insync.replicas=2`.
- Internal topic replication settings apply only when the internal topic is created. Get them right before the first client connects.
- Raising `message.max.bytes` requires matching changes on producers (`max.request.size`), and fetch limits on followers and consumers should be kept aligned.
- Check the effective configuration with `kafka-configs.sh --describe --all`, not just the properties file.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. (Beginner) Start a single broker with the sample configuration, produce to a topic that does not exist, and describe it. Then set `auto.create.topics.enable=false`, restart, and repeat. Record the client error you now get.
> 2. (Intermediate) Raise `message.max.bytes` to 5 MiB on a 3-broker cluster without changing `replica.fetch.max.bytes`, then produce a 4 MiB record with `acks=all`. Observe whether the followers keep up and stay in the ISR, and explain the result (look up how KIP-74 changed the handling of an oversized first batch in a fetch).
> 3. **Interview question:** "You inherit a cluster where `__consumer_offsets` has a replication factor of 1. How could that have happened, and how do you fix it without losing committed offsets?" *Hint: think about when internal topic settings are applied, and which tool changes the replica list of an existing topic.*

#### Dynamic Configuration

**Theory**

Restarting a broker is not free. It moves leadership, triggers replica catch-up, and, if the broker shut down uncleanly, starts a log recovery. Multiplied by a 30-broker cluster, a configuration change that requires a rolling restart can take hours. **Dynamic configuration** (introduced by KIP-226) lets you change many broker settings while the broker runs. Section 3.2 introduced the `kafka-configs.sh` tool and its precedence rules. This topic focuses on the operational side: which settings are dynamic, how changes are applied, and how to keep dynamic configuration from becoming invisible drift.

> Analogy: a running broker is an airplane in flight. Some parts (the engines' thread pools, the cabin temperature) can be adjusted mid-flight. Others (the wings, its `node.id` and `log.dirs`) can only be changed on the ground. The documentation tells you which is which.

**Update modes**

Every broker property has an update mode, listed in the Kafka documentation and returned by the Admin API:

| Update mode | Meaning | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| `read-only` | Requires a restart; cannot be set dynamically | `node.id`, `process.roles`, `log.dirs`, `broker.rack` |
| `per-broker` | Can be set for one broker (and usually as a cluster default) | `listeners`, `advertised.listeners`, `ssl.keystore.location`, `leader.replication.throttled.rate` |
| `cluster-wide` | Can be set as a cluster default and also per broker (useful for testing on one broker first) | `num.io.threads`, `num.network.threads`, `num.replica.fetchers`, `log.cleaner.threads`, `log.retention.ms`, `message.max.bytes`, `unclean.leader.election.enable`, `max.connections` |

**How a dynamic change is applied**

```text
 kafka-configs.sh / Admin API
        |  IncrementalAlterConfigs request
        v
 any broker  ---- forwards ---->  active controller
                                      |  validates, writes ConfigRecord to __cluster_metadata
                                      v
                        metadata log replicated to all brokers
                                      |
                 each broker applies the change in-process:
                 resize thread pool, reload keystore, update log config ...
```

Because the change is a record in the metadata log, it is durable, replicated, and applied to brokers that are offline when they come back. Brokers also validate it locally, and some changes (such as a keystore whose certificate does not match the listener) are rejected before they are stored.

**Operationally useful dynamic changes**

| Task | Setting | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Rotate TLS certificates without a restart | `listener.name.<l>.ssl.keystore.location` | Re-setting the **same path** forces a reload of the file (Section 11.1) |
| Add more request handler threads | `num.io.threads` | Applied immediately; watch `RequestHandlerAvgIdlePercent` |
| Speed up log compaction | `log.cleaner.threads`, `log.cleaner.io.max.bytes.per.second` | Cleaner threads restart with the new values |
| Throttle replication during reassignment | `leader.replication.throttled.rate`, `follower.replication.throttled.rate` | Set automatically by `kafka-reassign-partitions.sh --throttle` (Section 12.2) |
| Allow an emergency unclean election | `unclean.leader.election.enable` | Can be set per topic instead, to limit the blast radius |
| Raise a log level for debugging | `broker-loggers` entity | Remember to revert it (Section 3.2) |
| Add a listener | `listeners`, `advertised.listeners`, `listener.security.protocol.map` | Per broker; existing listeners cannot be removed while in use |

**Controller configuration**

In KRaft mode, controllers have their own configuration. Use `--bootstrap-controller` to talk to them directly:

```bash
# Describe the dynamic and static configuration of controller 1
bin/kafka-configs.sh --bootstrap-controller ctrl1:9093 --command-config admin.properties \
  --describe --entity-type brokers --entity-name 1 --all | head
```

**Example: changing thread pools on one broker, then cluster-wide**

```bash
BS=broker1:9092

# 1. Inspect the current value and its source
bin/kafka-configs.sh --bootstrap-server $BS --describe --broker 1 --all | grep num.io.threads
#   num.io.threads=8 sensitive=false synonyms={STATIC_BROKER_CONFIG:num.io.threads=8, DEFAULT_CONFIG:num.io.threads=8}

# 2. Canary: change it on broker 1 only, then watch RequestHandlerAvgIdlePercent for a while
bin/kafka-configs.sh --bootstrap-server $BS --alter --broker 1 --add-config num.io.threads=16

# 3. Roll it out as the cluster-wide default and remove the per-broker override
bin/kafka-configs.sh --bootstrap-server $BS --alter --broker-defaults --add-config num.io.threads=16
bin/kafka-configs.sh --bootstrap-server $BS --alter --broker 1 --delete-config num.io.threads
```

**Example: auditing configuration drift with the Admin API**

Dynamic configs silently override `server.properties`. Over time, nobody remembers why broker 7 has a different retention. A periodic report keeps drift visible:

```java
try (Admin admin = Admin.create(Map.of(AdminClientConfig.BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS_CONFIG, "broker1:9092"))) {
    List<ConfigResource> brokers = new ArrayList<>(admin.describeCluster().nodes().get().stream()
        .map(n -> new ConfigResource(ConfigResource.Type.BROKER, String.valueOf(n.id())))
        .toList());
    brokers.add(new ConfigResource(ConfigResource.Type.BROKER, ""));    // "" = cluster-wide defaults

    admin.describeConfigs(brokers).all().get().forEach((resource, config) ->
        config.entries().stream()
            .filter(e -> e.source() == ConfigEntry.ConfigSource.DYNAMIC_BROKER_CONFIG
                      || e.source() == ConfigEntry.ConfigSource.DYNAMIC_DEFAULT_BROKER_CONFIG)
            .forEach(e -> System.out.printf("broker=%s %s=%s (%s)%n",
                resource.name().isEmpty() ? "<default>" : resource.name(),
                e.name(), e.isSensitive() ? "******" : e.value(), e.source())));
}
```

**Keeping dynamic configuration manageable**

- Treat dynamic configs as code: manage them with a declarative tool (the Terraform Kafka provider, the Strimzi operator's `Kafka` resource, or a script in version control) rather than ad hoc CLI calls.
- Prefer topic-level overrides to broker-level ones when only some topics need a different value.
- Sensitive values (passwords, keys) are stored in the metadata log and returned as `null` with `sensitive=true` by describe calls. Protect metadata log directories and snapshots accordingly, and prefer config providers (`${file:...}`) for secrets.
- After an incident, remove temporary overrides (raised log levels, unclean election, throttles). A dynamic config outlives the incident that created it.

**Key Takeaways**

- Dynamic configs avoid rolling restarts. They are stored in the metadata log and survive broker restarts.
- Each property is `read-only`, `per-broker`, or `cluster-wide`. Check the documentation before planning a change.
- Canary a cluster-wide change on one broker first, then promote it to the cluster default.
- TLS keystores can be reloaded at runtime by re-setting the keystore location.
- Dynamic configs override `server.properties` without leaving a trace there. Audit them regularly and manage them declaratively.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. (Beginner) Change `log.cleaner.threads` dynamically on a running broker and find the log line in `log-cleaner.log` showing the cleaner restarting with the new value.
> 2. (Intermediate) Write a script that lists every dynamic broker override in the cluster and flags any key that is set per broker on fewer than all brokers.
> 3. **Interview question:** "You need to replace the TLS certificates on a 50-broker cluster before they expire tomorrow. How do you do it without a rolling restart, and how do you verify it worked?" *Hint: think about which entity and listener-prefixed key to change, what triggers the reload, and how to check the certificate actually served on each listener.*

#### Hardware and OS Tuning

**Theory**

Kafka's performance comes from cooperating with the operating system rather than working around it. Brokers append to files sequentially, rely on the **page cache** for reads (Section 7.1), and send data to consumers with zero-copy `sendfile`. That design means the hardware and kernel settings matter more than they do for many applications: a broker with plenty of CPU but too little memory for the page cache will hit disks constantly, and a broker with default file descriptor limits will crash once it hosts enough partitions.

> Analogy: Kafka is a fast courier service that uses the city's roads (the kernel) rather than building private ones. The courier is only as fast as the roads let it be, so you widen the roads it uses most: memory for caching, file handles, and network buffers.

**Sizing the main resources**

| Resource | What Kafka uses it for | Guidance |
|---|---|---|
| Memory | A small JVM heap (about 6 GB) plus the **page cache**, which holds recently written data so consumers read from memory | Leave most RAM to the OS. 64 GB per broker is a common size |
| Disk | Sequential appends and reads of log segments | Throughput matters more than IOPS for most workloads. See "Disk and Filesystem Choices" |
| Network | Producer traffic in, replication (RF-1 copies), consumer fan-out | Often the first bottleneck. 10 to 25 Gbit/s per broker is typical |
| CPU | Request handling, compression and decompression of mixed-codec batches, TLS encryption, CRC checks | Moderate. TLS and recompression raise it substantially |

**Estimating page cache needs**

The page cache should hold every byte that consumers are likely to read soon. A useful estimate is:

```text
 page cache needed per broker = (write throughput per broker) x (how far behind consumers may read, in seconds)

 Example: 150 MB/s of leader + follower writes per broker,
          consumers normally within 30 s of the head
          150 MB/s x 30 s = 4.5 GB  ->  comfortably served by a 64 GB machine with a 6 GB heap
```

Consumers that fall far behind read from disk instead, which is slower but still sequential. The danger is that cold reads evict hot data from the page cache and slow everyone else down.

**Network bandwidth budget**

```text
 Ingress per broker: produce traffic (P) + replication from leaders on other brokers ((RF-1) x P)
 Egress per broker:  replication to followers ((RF-1) x P) + consumer reads (P x number of consumer groups)

 P = 100 MB/s, RF = 3, 3 consumer groups
   ingress = 100 + 200 = 300 MB/s
   egress  = 200 + 300 = 500 MB/s  = 4 Gbit/s  -> a 10 Gbit/s NIC has headroom, a 1 Gbit/s NIC does not
```

**Kernel settings**

| Setting | Recommended | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `vm.swappiness` | `1` | Swapping a JVM heap causes multi-second pauses; keep swap as a last resort only |
| `vm.dirty_background_ratio` | `5` | Start background flushing of dirty pages early, in small steps |
| `vm.dirty_ratio` | `60` to `80` | Allow many dirty pages before writes block, since Kafka relies on replication rather than fsync for durability |
| `vm.max_map_count` | `262144` or more | Each log segment memory-maps two index files. The default of 65,530 limits a broker to roughly 32,000 segments before `Map failed` errors |
| File descriptors (`nofile`) | `100000` or more | One descriptor per segment file and per client connection |
| `net.core.rmem_max` / `wmem_max` | `16 MiB` or more | Allow larger socket buffers on high-bandwidth or high-latency links |
| `net.ipv4.tcp_rmem` / `tcp_wmem` | `4096 65536 16777216` | Auto-tuning range for TCP buffers |
| CPU frequency governor | `performance` | Avoid latency spikes from frequency scaling |

**Example: applying the settings**

```bash
# /etc/sysctl.d/90-kafka.conf
cat <<'EOF' | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/90-kafka.conf
vm.swappiness=1
vm.dirty_background_ratio=5
vm.dirty_ratio=60
vm.max_map_count=262144
net.core.rmem_max=16777216
net.core.wmem_max=16777216
net.ipv4.tcp_rmem=4096 65536 16777216
net.ipv4.tcp_wmem=4096 65536 16777216
EOF
sudo sysctl --system                       # apply without reboot
```

```ini
# /etc/systemd/system/kafka.service.d/limits.conf
# systemd ignores /etc/security/limits.conf for services; set limits on the unit instead
[Service]
LimitNOFILE=200000
LimitNPROC=65536
```

```bash
# Check the limits the running broker actually got, and how many descriptors it uses
PID=$(pgrep -f 'kafka\.Kafka')
grep 'open files' /proc/$PID/limits
ls /proc/$PID/fd | wc -l
wc -l < /proc/$PID/maps                    # compare with vm.max_map_count
```

**Other good practices**

- Run Kafka on dedicated machines (or dedicated nodes in Kubernetes). Co-located workloads compete for the page cache.
- Keep clocks synchronized with NTP or chrony. Time-based retention, timestamps, and log correlation all depend on it.
- Avoid huge latency differences between brokers: a cluster runs at the speed of its slowest ISR member when producers use `acks=all`.

**Key Takeaways**

- Kafka relies on the page cache, so give the heap a few GB and leave the rest of RAM to the OS.
- Budget network bandwidth for replication and consumer fan-out, not just produce traffic.
- Set `vm.swappiness=1`, raise `vm.max_map_count` and file descriptor limits, and tune dirty page ratios.
- Set limits on the systemd unit, then verify them on the running process through `/proc`.
- Use dedicated machines and synchronized clocks.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. (Beginner) On a test broker, check `vm.max_map_count`, `vm.swappiness`, and the broker process's open-file limit. Calculate how many segments the broker could memory-map before hitting the map limit.
> 2. (Intermediate) A cluster ingests 300 MB/s in total across 6 brokers with RF=3 and five consumer groups that each read everything. Compute the per-broker ingress and egress, and pick a NIC size with at least 40% headroom.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Why do Kafka operators usually recommend a small JVM heap on machines with lots of memory, when many other Java servers use as much heap as they can?" *Hint: think about where Kafka keeps recently written data and who manages that memory.*

#### JVM Tuning

**Theory**

Brokers and controllers are Java processes, so garbage collection (GC) pauses translate directly into latency for every client. A pause long enough to miss heartbeats can do more: a broker paused for longer than `broker.session.timeout.ms` (9 seconds by default in KRaft) is fenced by the controller and loses leadership, and a follower paused for longer than `replica.lag.time.max.ms` (30 seconds) drops out of the ISR. JVM tuning for Kafka aims at **short, predictable pauses** rather than maximum throughput.

The good news is that Kafka is easy on the heap. Record data mostly passes through the page cache and network buffers rather than living as Java objects, so a modest heap with a modern collector is enough.

> Analogy: the JVM heap is the broker's desk, the page cache its filing cabinet. A bigger desk does not make the clerk faster. It only makes tidying the desk (garbage collection) take longer. Kafka keeps a small, tidy desk and a huge filing cabinet.

**Recommended baseline (Java 17 or 21, G1 collector)**

| Option | Value | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `-Xms` / `-Xmx` | Equal, about `6g` for brokers (4 to 8 GB) | Equal values avoid heap resizing; more heap steals page cache |
| Collector | `-XX:+UseG1GC` (the default in Kafka's scripts) | Region-based, pause-time goal, mature |
| `-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis` | `20` | Pause-time target G1 tries to meet |
| `-XX:InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent` | `35` | Start concurrent marking early to avoid full GCs |
| `-XX:G1HeapRegionSize` | `16M` | Fewer "humongous" allocations for large request buffers |
| `-XX:MetaspaceSize` | `96m` | Avoid early metaspace-triggered collections |
| `-XX:+ExplicitGCInvokesConcurrent` | enabled | `System.gc()` calls (for example from direct buffer cleanup) run concurrently |
| GC logging | `-Xlog:gc*:file=...:time,tags:filecount=10,filesize=100M` | Required to diagnose any pause |

Controllers usually need less heap than brokers (2 to 4 GB is common), since they keep the cluster metadata in memory but serve no client data. Very large clusters (hundreds of thousands of partitions) need more.

**Configuring the JVM through environment variables**

Kafka's start scripts read a few environment variables, so you do not edit the scripts themselves:

| Variable | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `KAFKA_HEAP_OPTS` | Heap size (`-Xms`, `-Xmx`) |
| `KAFKA_JVM_PERFORMANCE_OPTS` | Collector and GC tuning flags (replaces Kafka's default set) |
| `KAFKA_GC_LOG_OPTS` | GC logging flags (used when the start script passes `-loggc`, as `kafka-server-start.sh` does) |
| `KAFKA_JMX_OPTS` / `JMX_PORT` | Remote JMX (Section 12.3) |
| `KAFKA_OPTS` | Anything else, for example a `-javaagent` for metrics |

**Example: a systemd unit for a broker**

```ini
# /etc/systemd/system/kafka.service
[Unit]
Description=Apache Kafka broker
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
User=kafka
Environment="KAFKA_HEAP_OPTS=-Xms6g -Xmx6g"
Environment="KAFKA_JVM_PERFORMANCE_OPTS=-server -XX:+UseG1GC -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=20 \
  -XX:InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent=35 -XX:G1HeapRegionSize=16M -XX:MetaspaceSize=96m \
  -XX:MinMetaspaceFreeRatio=50 -XX:MaxMetaspaceFreeRatio=80 -XX:+ExplicitGCInvokesConcurrent \
  -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/var/log/kafka/heapdump.hprof"
Environment="KAFKA_GC_LOG_OPTS=-Xlog:gc*:file=/var/log/kafka/gc.log:time,tags:filecount=10,filesize=100M"
Environment="LOG_DIR=/var/log/kafka"
ExecStart=/opt/kafka/bin/kafka-server-start.sh /etc/kafka/broker.properties
ExecStop=/opt/kafka/bin/kafka-server-stop.sh
TimeoutStopSec=300          # give controlled shutdown time to move leadership
Restart=on-failure
LimitNOFILE=200000

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```

`TimeoutStopSec` matters: if systemd kills the broker with SIGKILL before controlled shutdown finishes, the next start performs log recovery.

**Reading GC logs**

```text
[2026-10-23T09:12:44.118+0000][gc] GC(4512) Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 3712M->1104M(6144M) 11.384ms
[2026-10-23T09:12:51.902+0000][gc] GC(4513) Pause Young (Concurrent Start) (G1 Humongous Allocation) 2950M->1210M(6144M) 14.920ms
[2026-10-23T09:13:20.441+0000][gc] GC(4520) Pause Full (G1 Compaction Pause) 6120M->5980M(6144M) 4231.551ms
```

The first two lines are healthy young collections around 10 to 15 ms. The last is a **full GC** that freed almost nothing and paused for over 4 seconds: the live data does not fit in the heap. The fix is to find what is consuming heap (too many partitions or connections for the heap size, or a memory leak) and size the heap accordingly, not to tune G1 flags.

```bash
# Quick live view of GC activity without restarting: sample every 5 seconds
jstat -gcutil $(pgrep -f 'kafka\.Kafka') 5000
```

**Other collectors**

Generational ZGC (Java 21) delivers sub-millisecond pauses largely independent of heap size, at the cost of more CPU and memory overhead. It can make sense for latency-sensitive clusters with large heaps, but G1 remains the well-tested default. Whatever you choose, test it under production-like load before rolling it out.

**Key Takeaways**

- GC pauses become client latency, and long pauses cause fencing and ISR shrinks.
- Use G1 with a 4 to 8 GB heap (equal `-Xms`/`-Xmx`) for brokers. Controllers need less.
- Configure the JVM through `KAFKA_HEAP_OPTS`, `KAFKA_JVM_PERFORMANCE_OPTS`, and `KAFKA_GC_LOG_OPTS`.
- Always enable GC logging and heap dumps on out-of-memory errors.
- Repeated full GCs mean the live set does not fit in the heap. Fix the cause or resize the heap rather than tuning flags.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. (Beginner) Start a broker with GC logging enabled, run `kafka-producer-perf-test.sh` against it for two minutes, and report the maximum young-GC pause from the log.
> 2. (Intermediate) Run the same test with `-Xmx512m` and with `-Xmx6g`. Compare GC frequency, pause times, and producer latency percentiles, and explain the differences.
> 3. **Interview question:** "A broker periodically drops out of the ISR for every partition it follows and then rejoins a minute later. CPU and disk look normal. What would you look at first?" *Hint: think about what makes a whole JVM stop responding for seconds, and which log would prove it.*

#### Disk and Filesystem Choices

**Theory**

Every record a broker accepts is written to disk, every replica is another copy on another disk, and every consumer that falls out of the page cache reads from disk. Storage is usually the most expensive part of a Kafka cluster and the most common cause of incidents (full disks, slow disks, failed disks). The choices to make are the **media** (HDD, SSD, network-attached), the **layout** (JBOD or RAID), and the **filesystem**.

Because Kafka writes sequentially and replicates data itself, its needs differ from those of a database. It does not need RAID for redundancy (replication already provides it) and does not need high random IOPS for normal operation (writes are appends). It does need sustained sequential throughput, enough capacity, and predictable latency.

**Media**

| Media | Strengths | Weaknesses | Fits |
|---|---|---|---|
| HDD | Cheap per TB, good sequential throughput | Slow when many partitions or lagging consumers cause seeks | Large retention, few partitions per disk |
| SATA/SAS SSD | Consistent latency, good mixed workloads | Higher cost per TB | General purpose |
| NVMe SSD | Very high throughput and low latency | Highest cost | Low-latency, high-partition-count clusters |
| Cloud block storage (EBS gp3, Azure Premium SSD, GCP PD) | Survives instance loss, resizable | Throughput and IOPS caps per volume; network-attached latency | Most cloud deployments |
| Cloud instance storage (local NVMe) | Fastest, no per-volume caps | Data lost when the instance stops | When replication plus fast re-replication is acceptable |

With tiered storage (Section 7.3), local disks only hold recent data, so smaller and faster disks become affordable.

**Layout: JBOD vs RAID**

| Layout | How it works | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|---|
| **JBOD** (several `log.dirs`) | Each disk is a separate log directory; Kafka places partitions across them | Full capacity and throughput of every disk; a failed disk takes only its partitions offline | Partitions are not balanced by size automatically; one hot partition can fill one disk |
| **RAID 10** | Mirrored stripes presented as one volume | Disk failure invisible to Kafka; balanced I/O | Half the capacity; replication already gives redundancy, so data is stored 2 x RF times |
| **RAID 0** | Stripes without redundancy | One big fast volume | One disk failure loses the whole volume |
| **RAID 5/6** | Parity | More capacity than RAID 10 | Poor write performance and very slow rebuilds. Avoid |

JBOD is the most common choice for new clusters. KRaft mode supports it since Kafka 3.7 (KIP-858): when one directory fails, the broker reports it to the controller, leadership of affected partitions moves to other brokers, and the broker keeps serving partitions on its healthy disks.

**Filesystem**

- **XFS** is the most widely recommended filesystem for Kafka: it handles large files and parallel appends well and needs no special tuning.
- **ext4** also works well. Avoid mount options that trade safety for speed (such as disabling barriers) unless you fully understand the consequences.
- Mount with **`noatime`** so reads do not trigger metadata writes for access times.
- Do **not** use network filesystems such as NFS for log directories. Kafka relies on file locking and memory-mapped indexes that NFS handles poorly.
- Put the **metadata log** (`metadata.log.dir`) on a separate, reliable disk on combined or controller nodes, and keep OS, application logs, and GC logs off the data disks.

**Example: preparing data disks on a broker**

```bash
# Format three data disks with XFS and mount them with noatime
for i in 1 2 3; do
  dev=/dev/nvme${i}n1
  sudo mkfs.xfs -f -L kafka-$i "$dev"
  sudo mkdir -p /data/kafka-$i
  echo "LABEL=kafka-$i /data/kafka-$i xfs defaults,noatime 0 0" | sudo tee -a /etc/fstab
done
sudo mount -a
sudo chown -R kafka:kafka /data/kafka-*
```

```properties
# broker.properties
log.dirs=/data/kafka-1,/data/kafka-2,/data/kafka-3
```

**Example: inspecting and rebalancing directories**

```bash
# Size of every partition replica on broker 4, per log directory (JSON output)
bin/kafka-log-dirs.sh --bootstrap-server broker4:9092 --describe --broker-list 4 \
  | tail -1 | jq -r '.brokers[].logDirs[] | "\(.logDir) \([.partitions[].size] | add / 1e9 | floor) GB"'
# /data/kafka-1 812 GB
# /data/kafka-2 301 GB
# /data/kafka-3 655 GB
```

Moving a replica between directories on the same broker uses the same reassignment tool as moving it between brokers, with a `log_dirs` field:

```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "partitions": [
    { "topic": "clickstream", "partition": 7, "replicas": [4, 2, 6],
      "log_dirs": ["/data/kafka-2", "any", "any"] }
  ]
}
```

```bash
# Intra-broker moves have their own throttle
bin/kafka-reassign-partitions.sh --bootstrap-server broker4:9092 \
  --reassignment-json-file move-dir.json --execute --replica-alter-log-dirs-throttle 100000000
```

**Key Takeaways**

- Kafka needs sequential throughput and capacity more than random IOPS. Replication replaces RAID for redundancy.
- JBOD gives full capacity and isolates disk failures. RAID 10 is simpler to operate but halves capacity. Avoid RAID 5/6.
- Use XFS (or ext4) with `noatime`. Never use NFS.
- Keep the metadata log, OS, and logs off the data disks.
- Watch per-directory usage with `kafka-log-dirs.sh` and move replicas between directories with `log_dirs` in a reassignment.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. (Beginner) Configure a broker with two log directories, create a topic with 8 partitions, and use `kafka-log-dirs.sh` to see how partitions were placed.
> 2. (Intermediate) Fill one directory much faster than the other by producing only to partitions placed there. Then write and execute a reassignment that moves two of those replicas to the other directory with a throttle, and verify the result.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Would you run Kafka on RAID 10, RAID 5, or JBOD? Defend your answer for a cluster with RF=3 on bare metal." *Hint: consider usable capacity, what happens during a disk failure and a rebuild, and what redundancy Kafka already provides.*

<a id="122-cluster-maintenance"></a>
### 12.2 Cluster Maintenance

A Kafka cluster is never finished: brokers need patches, Kafka needs upgrades, the cluster grows and shrinks, and load drifts out of balance. This section covers the routine procedures that keep it healthy without interrupting clients, and Cruise Control, the tool that automates much of the rebalancing work.

#### Rolling Restarts

**Theory**

Almost every maintenance task (OS patches, JVM changes, static configuration changes, upgrades) ends with "and then restart the brokers". Restarting all of them at once would make every partition unavailable. A **rolling restart** restarts one node at a time and waits for the cluster to be fully healthy again before moving on. Because every partition has replicas on other brokers (Section 2.4), clients barely notice: leadership moves away from the stopping broker, the remaining ISR members keep serving, and the restarted broker catches up before the next one stops.

> Analogy: replacing the tires on a moving bus is impossible, but a bus with three spare axles can lift one wheel at a time, swap it, and lower it again, as long as you never lift a second wheel before the first one is back on the road.

**What happens during a clean stop**

```text
 SIGTERM to broker 2
   |
   v
 controlled shutdown: broker 2 tells the controller it wants to shut down (heartbeat flag)
   |
   v
 controller moves leadership of every partition led by broker 2 to another ISR member
 and removes broker 2 from ISRs (metadata records committed)
   |
   v
 broker 2 flushes logs, writes the clean-shutdown marker, exits
   |                                         clients: NOT_LEADER_OR_FOLLOWER -> refresh metadata -> retry
   v
 restart: broker 2 loads logs (fast, because the shutdown was clean), registers, fetches metadata
   |
   v
 broker 2 catches up as a follower and rejoins each ISR  ->  under-replicated partitions back to 0
```

If the broker is killed (SIGKILL, power loss) instead, leadership moves only after the session timeout, and on restart the broker must **recover** every segment written since the last checkpoint, which can take many minutes on brokers with large logs.

**The safety rule**

Only stop the next node when:

1. **No partition is under-replicated** (`UnderReplicatedPartitions` = 0 on every broker), and
2. **The controller quorum is healthy**: all voters are caught up with the leader.

Stopping a second broker while some partitions still have only two ISR members can push them below `min.insync.replicas`, which blocks `acks=all` producers, or make them offline altogether.

**Order of restarts in a KRaft cluster**

| Step | Nodes | Why |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Controllers that are **not** the active controller, one at a time | Keep the active controller stable as long as possible |
| 2 | The active controller | Causes exactly one controller election |
| 3 | Brokers, one at a time | Leadership moves between ISR members |

In combined mode (`process.roles=broker,controller`), each node is both, so restart the nodes one at a time, leaving the active controller's node for last.

**Example: a rolling restart script**

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# rolling-restart.sh: restart brokers one at a time, waiting for full health between each
set -euo pipefail
BS=broker1:9092
CFG=admin.properties
BROKERS=(broker1 broker2 broker3 broker4 broker5 broker6)

urp_count() {
  # Partitions whose ISR is smaller than the replica list
  bin/kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server "$BS" --command-config "$CFG" \
    --describe --under-replicated-partitions | grep -c "Partition:" || true
}

wait_healthy() {
  for _ in $(seq 1 120); do                      # up to 20 minutes
    if [[ "$(urp_count)" -eq 0 ]]; then return 0; fi
    sleep 10
  done
  echo "cluster did not become healthy, aborting" >&2; exit 1
}

wait_healthy                                      # never start on an unhealthy cluster
for host in "${BROKERS[@]}"; do
  echo "== restarting $host"
  ssh "$host" 'sudo systemctl restart kafka'      # SIGTERM -> controlled shutdown -> start
  sleep 30                                        # let it register before checking
  wait_healthy
  echo "== $host healthy"
done
```

**Checking the controller quorum**

```bash
bin/kafka-metadata-quorum.sh --bootstrap-server broker1:9092 describe --status
# ClusterId:              5L6g3nShT-eMCtK--X86sw
# LeaderId:               2                      <- active controller: restart it last
# LeaderEpoch:            41
# HighWatermark:          1849302
# MaxFollowerLag:         0
# CurrentVoters:          [{"id": 1, ...}, {"id": 2, ...}, {"id": 3, ...}]
# CurrentObservers:       [{"id": 4, ...}, ...]

bin/kafka-metadata-quorum.sh --bootstrap-server broker1:9092 describe --replication
# NodeId  DirectoryId             LogEndOffset  Lag  LastFetchTimestamp  LastCaughtUpTimestamp  Status
# 2       pgCGpQ6sQ2SgOgYIcc8mEw  1849302       0    1761210942120       1761210942120          Leader
# 1       Zc8ZQ1eVRe6Q0FqCtQq3hA  1849302       0    1761210942010       1761210942010          Follower
# 3       x5a1bS-kQ4Sbn2pT0X2fJg  1849301       1    1761210942020       1761210942020          Follower
```

**Practical tips**

- Give controlled shutdown enough time (`TimeoutStopSec` in systemd, `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` in Kubernetes). A broker leading thousands of partitions may need a minute or more.
- After the last broker, leadership is unbalanced: the last brokers restarted lead nothing. Automatic leader rebalancing (topic "Preferred Leader Election") fixes this within minutes, or trigger it yourself.
- On Kubernetes, operators such as Strimzi perform rolling restarts with these checks built in (Section 14.3).

**Key Takeaways**

- Restart one node at a time and wait for zero under-replicated partitions and a caught-up quorum before the next.
- Use SIGTERM so controlled shutdown moves leadership first. Killed brokers recover logs slowly on restart.
- In KRaft, restart non-active controllers first, then the active controller, then the brokers.
- Automate the health checks in a script so nobody skips them under time pressure.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. (Beginner) On a 3-broker local cluster, run a producer with `acks=all` in a loop and restart one broker with SIGTERM. Then repeat with SIGKILL. Compare the producer's error output and the restart times.
> 2. (Intermediate) Extend the script to also check `--under-min-isr-partitions` and the quorum's `MaxFollowerLag`, and to abort if any broker is not registered after restart (hint: `kafka-broker-api-versions.sh` lists reachable brokers).
> 3. **Interview question:** "During a rolling restart, a colleague restarts the next broker as soon as the previous one's process is up. What can go wrong?" *Hint: being up is not the same as being in sync. Think about which partitions now have fewer in-sync copies than usual.*

#### Rolling Upgrades

**Theory**

Upgrading Kafka is a rolling restart with new binaries, plus one extra concern: **compatibility during the transition**. For a while, old and new versions run side by side, so new versions must not use features that old nodes do not understand. Kafka solves this with **feature versions**. The binaries are upgraded first, while the cluster keeps behaving like the old version. Only when every node runs the new software do you **finalize** the upgrade by raising the cluster's feature levels, which enables the new on-disk and protocol formats.

> Analogy: when a city switches to a new kind of train ticket, it first installs readers that accept both old and new tickets at every station. Only when every station has the new reader does it start selling new tickets. Selling them earlier would strand passengers at stations with old readers.

**Feature versions in KRaft**

| Feature | Controls |
|---|---|
| `metadata.version` | Format of records in the metadata log and related broker-controller behavior |
| `kraft.version` | Raft protocol features, such as dynamic controller membership (3.9+) |
| `group.version` | New consumer group protocol (KIP-848) |
| `transaction.version` | Transaction protocol improvements (KIP-890) |
| `eligible.leader.replicas.version` | Eligible Leader Replicas (KIP-966, Section 2.4) |
| `share.version` | Share groups (Section 5.4) |

Each node advertises the range of levels it supports. The controller only lets you finalize a level that every registered node supports.

**The upgrade procedure**

```text
 1. Prepare        read the upgrade notes for every version you skip; check client versions,
                   Java version, removed configs; test in staging with production-like load
 2. Roll binaries  controllers first (non-active, then active), then brokers; one node at a time,
                   waiting for full health after each (same rules as a rolling restart)
                   -> cluster runs new code with OLD feature levels: downgrading binaries is still possible
 3. Soak           run for days; compare latency, throughput, error rates, GC with the baseline
 4. Finalize       kafka-features.sh upgrade --release-version <new>
                   -> new formats enabled; usually no way back
```

Step 4 is the **point of no return**: downgrading `metadata.version` is generally not supported, so a cluster finalized at a new level cannot go back to older binaries. Do not finalize until the soak period has given you confidence.

**Example: upgrading from 4.0 to 4.1**

```bash
BS=broker1:9092

# Before: what does the cluster support, and what is finalized?
bin/kafka-features.sh --bootstrap-server $BS describe
# Feature: metadata.version   SupportedMinVersion: 3.3-IV3  SupportedMaxVersion: 4.0-IV3  FinalizedVersionLevel: 4.0-IV3 ...
# (values illustrative; after all nodes run 4.1, SupportedMaxVersion shows the 4.1 level)

# Per node: stop, swap binaries, start, wait for health
ssh broker1 'sudo systemctl stop kafka && sudo ln -sfn /opt/kafka_2.13-4.1.0 /opt/kafka && sudo systemctl start kafka'
# ... wait for under-replicated partitions = 0, then the next node ...

# Which feature levels does a release correspond to?
bin/kafka-features.sh --bootstrap-server $BS version-mapping --release-version 4.1

# Preview, then finalize, after the soak period
bin/kafka-features.sh --bootstrap-server $BS upgrade --release-version 4.1 --dry-run
bin/kafka-features.sh --bootstrap-server $BS upgrade --release-version 4.1
```

Using a symlink such as `/opt/kafka` that points to a versioned directory makes both the upgrade and a binary rollback a one-line change.

**Compatibility checks before upgrading**

| Area | What to check |
|---|---|
| Clients | Kafka 4.0 removed old protocol versions (KIP-896): clients older than 2.1 cannot connect. Check `kafka.network:type=RequestMetrics,name=RequestsPerSec,request=*,version=*` for old API versions in use |
| Java | Kafka 4.x brokers require Java 17+; clients require Java 11+ |
| Metadata mode | 4.x runs only in KRaft. ZooKeeper clusters must migrate on 3.9 first (Section 2.3) |
| Configuration | Removed or renamed properties make the broker fail at startup. Search the upgrade notes for "removed" |
| Logging | Kafka 4.0 moved to Log4j 2 (`log4j2.yaml`); custom `log4j.properties` files must be converted |
| Ecosystem | Connect plugins, Streams applications, Schema Registry, monitoring agents: each has its own compatibility matrix |

Clients and brokers are **bidirectionally compatible** across a wide range of versions (Chapter 16): an old client talks to a new broker and vice versa, negotiating API versions with the `ApiVersions` request. Upgrade brokers first, then clients at your own pace.

**Rolling back**

| Situation | Rollback |
|---|---|
| Problem during step 2 or 3 (not finalized) | Roll the old binaries back the same way, one node at a time |
| Problem after step 4 (finalized) | No binary downgrade. Fix forward with a patch release, configuration changes, or support |

**Key Takeaways**

- Upgrades are a rolling restart with new binaries followed by a separate finalization step.
- Feature versions (`metadata.version` and friends) keep a mixed-version cluster compatible until you finalize.
- Finalizing is effectively irreversible. Soak first, and keep the old binaries ready until then.
- Check clients, Java, configuration, logging, and ecosystem compatibility before you start.
- Upgrade brokers before clients. The protocol negotiates versions automatically.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. (Beginner) Run `kafka-features.sh describe` on a local cluster and explain each feature's supported range and finalized level.
> 2. (Intermediate) Set up a 3-node cluster on an older 4.x release, produce and consume continuously, and upgrade it to the latest release without the console consumer seeing a gap or duplicate. Document each step and the health checks you used.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Your team wants to finalize the metadata version immediately after rolling out new binaries, to get a new feature. What would you say?" *Hint: separate what can still be rolled back before and after finalization, and what evidence you would want first.*

#### Partition Reassignment

**Theory**

A partition's **replica assignment** (the list of brokers that hold its replicas) is chosen when the topic is created and never changes on its own. Kafka does **not** move data automatically when you add brokers, remove brokers, or when some partitions grow much faster than others. **Partition reassignment** is the mechanism to change assignments: it copies the data to the new replicas in the background and switches over only when they are fully caught up. Section 2.4 used it to change a replication factor. This topic covers the full workflow and how to do it safely at scale.

> Analogy: moving offices without closing the business. You set up the new desks and copy every file there while staff keep working at the old desks. Only when the new office is fully in sync do people move, and only then are the old desks removed.

**How a reassignment progresses**

```text
 Partition orders-3: current replicas [1, 2, 3], target [1, 2, 4]

 1. Start        replicas = [1, 2, 3, 4]   adding = [4]   removing = [3]
                 broker 4 starts fetching from the leader, from the log start offset
 2. Catch-up     broker 4 copies the whole partition (may take hours for large partitions)
 3. Join ISR     broker 4 is caught up -> ISR = [1, 2, 3, 4]
 4. Switch       controller sets replicas = [1, 2, 4] (and moves leadership if the leader is being removed)
 5. Clean up     broker 3 stops replicating and deletes its copy
```

During steps 1 to 3, the partition has **more** replicas than usual, so the cluster temporarily needs extra disk space and extra replication bandwidth. That extra traffic competes with client traffic, which is why reassignments must be **throttled**.

**The tool: `kafka-reassign-partitions.sh`**

| Mode | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `--generate` | Propose a new assignment for given topics over a given broker list (simple round-robin; ignores load) |
| `--execute` | Start the reassignment described in a JSON file. Prints the current assignment first: **save it** for rollback |
| `--verify` | Report progress. When complete, removes the throttles (unless `--preserve-throttles`) |
| `--list` | Show all reassignments in progress |
| `--cancel` | Stop in-progress reassignments and revert to the original replicas |
| `--additional` | Add new reassignments while others are still running |

**Throttling**

`--throttle <bytes/s>` limits the replication traffic used by moving replicas. It sets dynamic configs on the brokers (`leader.replication.throttled.rate`, `follower.replication.throttled.rate`) and on the topics (`leader.replication.throttled.replicas`, `follower.replication.throttled.replicas`) so that only the moving replicas are throttled, not normal replication. Choose the rate from your network headroom:

```text
 NIC 10 Gbit/s = ~1,250 MB/s; peak client + normal replication traffic = 700 MB/s
 keep 30% headroom -> available ~ 1,250 x 0.7 - 700 = ~175 MB/s  -> --throttle 150000000
```

If the throttle is lower than the partition's produce rate, the new replica can never catch up. Watch the `ReassignmentBytesInPerSec` and `ReassignmentBytesOutPerSec` broker metrics and raise the throttle if progress stalls.

**Example: spreading three topics onto a newly added broker 7**

```bash
BS=broker1:9092

# 1. Generate a proposal for the topics over brokers 1-7
cat > topics.json <<'EOF'
{ "version": 1, "topics": [ {"topic": "orders"}, {"topic": "payments"}, {"topic": "clickstream"} ] }
EOF
bin/kafka-reassign-partitions.sh --bootstrap-server $BS \
  --topics-to-move-json-file topics.json --broker-list 1,2,3,4,5,6,7 --generate
# Current partition replica assignment   {...}   -> save as rollback.json
# Proposed partition reassignment configuration {...}   -> save as plan.json, then review and trim it

# 2. Execute with a throttle; the tool prints the current assignment again for rollback
bin/kafka-reassign-partitions.sh --bootstrap-server $BS \
  --reassignment-json-file plan.json --execute --throttle 150000000

# 3. Watch progress
bin/kafka-reassign-partitions.sh --bootstrap-server $BS --reassignment-json-file plan.json --verify
# Status of partition reassignment:
# Reassignment of partition orders-0 is completed.
# Reassignment of partition clickstream-11 is still in progress.

bin/kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server $BS --describe --topic clickstream | grep "Adding"
#   Topic: clickstream  Partition: 11  Leader: 3  Replicas: 3,5,1,7  Isr: 3,5,1  Adding Replicas: 7  Removing Replicas: 1

# 4. Raise the throttle without restarting the reassignment, if needed
bin/kafka-reassign-partitions.sh --bootstrap-server $BS \
  --reassignment-json-file plan.json --execute --additional --throttle 250000000

# 5. When --verify reports everything completed, it also removes the throttle configs
```

**Planning reassignments safely**

- **Review `--generate` output.** It can move far more partitions than necessary, because it reshuffles every listed topic. Hand-edit the plan or use a tool that minimizes movement (Cruise Control).
- **Move in batches.** A plan with hundreds of large partitions takes hours to days and needs extra disk on targets the whole time. Run batches of a manageable size.
- **Keep preferred leaders balanced.** The first broker in each replica list is the preferred leader (next topic). Rotate it across brokers.
- **Respect racks.** `--generate` is rack-aware by default. Hand-written plans must keep replicas of a partition in different racks.
- **Check disk space on targets** before starting: they receive full copies.
- **Keep the rollback file.** Executing it (or `--cancel` while in progress) restores the original placement.

**Example: the Admin API**

```java
try (Admin admin = Admin.create(Map.of(AdminClientConfig.BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS_CONFIG, "broker1:9092"))) {
    // Move orders-3 from [1,2,3] to [1,2,4]
    admin.alterPartitionReassignments(Map.of(
        new TopicPartition("orders", 3),
        Optional.of(new NewPartitionReassignment(List.of(1, 2, 4)))
    )).all().get();

    // Report reassignments still in progress
    admin.listPartitionReassignments().reassignments().get().forEach((tp, r) ->
        System.out.printf("%s replicas=%s adding=%s removing=%s%n",
            tp, r.replicas(), r.addingReplicas(), r.removingReplicas()));

    // Optional.empty() cancels a reassignment and reverts to the original replicas
    // admin.alterPartitionReassignments(Map.of(new TopicPartition("orders", 3), Optional.empty()));
}
```

The Admin API does not set throttles. Set the throttle configs yourself with `incrementalAlterConfigs` when you use it.

**Key Takeaways**

- Kafka never rebalances data on its own. Reassignment changes which brokers hold each partition, copying data first and switching after.
- During a move, partitions temporarily have extra replicas: plan disk space and bandwidth for them.
- Always throttle, and pick a rate above the partition's produce rate but within network headroom. `--verify` removes the throttle at the end.
- Save the current assignment as a rollback plan. `--cancel` reverts in-progress moves.
- Move in batches, keep racks and preferred leaders balanced, and review generated plans before executing them.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. (Beginner) On a 3-broker cluster, add a fourth broker, then use `--generate` and `--execute` to move half of a topic's replicas onto it. Watch the `Adding Replicas` field until the move completes.
> 2. (Intermediate) Produce continuously at 20 MB/s to a partition while moving it with `--throttle 5000000`. Observe what happens, explain why the move never completes, and fix it without cancelling.
> 3. **Interview question:** "You added three brokers to a 9-broker cluster a month ago, and they are almost idle. Why, and how do you fix it with minimal disruption?" *Hint: Kafka does not move existing partitions automatically. Think about how many partitions to move, in what order, and how to protect clients during the move.*

#### Preferred Leader Election

**Theory**

Every partition has a **preferred leader**: the first broker in its replica list. When topics are created, Kafka spreads first replicas evenly across brokers so that each broker leads a similar share of partitions. Leaders do most of the work (they handle all produce requests and most consumer fetches), so balanced leadership means balanced load.

Over time, leadership drifts. Every failover and every controlled shutdown moves leadership to another ISR member, and nothing moves it back automatically at that moment. After a rolling restart, the last broker restarted may lead no partitions at all while the first leads twice its share. **Preferred leader election** moves leadership back to the preferred replica for every partition where it is in the ISR.

> Analogy: each team has a designated captain (the preferred leader). When the captain leaves the field, someone else wears the armband. When the captain returns, the referee gives the armband back, but only once the captain is fully warmed up (back in the ISR).

**Leader imbalance after a rolling restart**

```text
                  Partitions led (preferred share = 100 each)
 Broker   before restart    after rolling restart    after preferred election
   1           100                 150                        100
   2           100                 125                        100
   3           100                  25                        100   <- restarted last
```

**Automatic rebalancing**

Brokers rebalance leadership on their own when these settings allow it:

| Setting | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `auto.leader.rebalance.enable` | `true` | The controller periodically triggers preferred elections |
| `leader.imbalance.check.interval.seconds` | `300` | How often the controller checks |
| `leader.imbalance.per.broker.percentage` | `10` | Trigger elections for a broker only when more than this percentage of its preferred partitions are led by someone else |

With these defaults, leadership returns to balance within about five minutes after a restart. Some operators disable automatic rebalancing on very large or latency-sensitive clusters and trigger elections at controlled times instead, since every election causes a brief metadata refresh and retry on clients.

**Manual elections with `kafka-leader-election.sh`**

```bash
BS=broker1:9092

# All partitions whose preferred leader is in the ISR but not leading
bin/kafka-leader-election.sh --bootstrap-server $BS --election-type PREFERRED --all-topic-partitions

# A single partition
bin/kafka-leader-election.sh --bootstrap-server $BS --election-type PREFERRED --topic orders --partition 3

# A list of partitions from a file, for example to rebalance in small batches
cat > elect.json <<'EOF'
{ "partitions": [ {"topic": "orders", "partition": 0}, {"topic": "payments", "partition": 5} ] }
EOF
bin/kafka-leader-election.sh --bootstrap-server $BS --election-type PREFERRED --path-to-json-file elect.json
```

The same tool also runs `--election-type UNCLEAN` (Section 2.4), a different and dangerous operation used only to recover offline partitions.

**Measuring imbalance**

- The controller metric `kafka.controller:type=KafkaController,name=PreferredReplicaImbalanceCount` counts partitions not led by their preferred replica. Expect it to be near zero in steady state.
- Per-broker `kafka.server:type=ReplicaManager,name=LeaderCount` shows how many partitions each broker leads.

```bash
# Count leaders per broker from the topic description
bin/kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server broker1:9092 --describe \
  | awk '/Partition:/ { for (i = 1; i <= NF; i++) if ($i == "Leader:") print $(i+1) }' \
  | sort | uniq -c | sort -k2 -n
#    101 1
#    148 2
#     51 3
```

**When preferred election is not enough**

Preferred election can only restore the balance that the **assignment** describes. If preferred leaders were never balanced (hand-written reassignments that always list the same broker first, or brokers added later), balanced elections still produce unbalanced load. The fix is a reassignment that reorders replica lists, which is also what Cruise Control's `PreferredLeaderElectionGoal` and leader-distribution goals do. Likewise, leader count is a proxy: 100 leaders of idle partitions weigh less than 10 leaders of hot ones.

**Key Takeaways**

- The preferred leader is the first replica in the assignment. Balanced preferred leaders mean balanced leader load.
- Failovers and restarts unbalance leadership. Preferred elections move it back once the preferred replica is in the ISR.
- `auto.leader.rebalance.enable=true` does this every 5 minutes when imbalance exceeds 10% per broker.
- Use `kafka-leader-election.sh --election-type PREFERRED` for manual or batched elections.
- If the assignment itself is unbalanced, reorder replica lists with a reassignment.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. (Beginner) Disable `auto.leader.rebalance.enable`, restart brokers one by one on a 3-broker cluster, and count leaders per broker. Then run a preferred election and count again.
> 2. (Intermediate) Write a reassignment JSON for a 6-partition topic on brokers 1 to 3 in which broker 1 is the preferred leader of four partitions. Apply it, run a preferred election, and show that leadership stays unbalanced. Then fix the replica order.
> 3. **Interview question:** "Why doesn't Kafka immediately give leadership back to a broker the moment it restarts?" *Hint: think about what the returning broker's log looks like right after startup, and what would happen to `acks=all` producers and consumers if it led too early.*

#### Decommissioning Brokers

**Theory**

Sooner or later a broker has to leave the cluster permanently: hardware is retired, the cluster is downsized, or instances are migrated to a new machine type. Simply shutting the broker down is not decommissioning. Its partitions would stay assigned to it and remain **under-replicated forever**, with one copy fewer than intended. Proper decommissioning first moves every replica off the broker while it is still running, then stops it, and finally removes it from the cluster's metadata.

> Analogy: an employee leaving a company does not just stop showing up. They hand over every project to colleagues first, then return their badge. The handover is the reassignment, the badge is the broker registration.

**The procedure**

```text
 1. Check capacity   Can the remaining brokers absorb the departing broker's data, traffic, and leaders?
 2. Drain            Reassign every replica on the broker to other brokers (throttled, in batches)
 3. Verify empty     The broker hosts no replicas and leads no partitions
 4. Stop             Shut down the broker process
 5. Unregister       Remove the broker registration from the cluster metadata (KRaft)
 6. Clean up         Update bootstrap lists, DNS, monitoring, firewall rules, certificates
```

Draining a busy broker can take hours, but clients see nothing more than leadership moves. Throttling applies exactly as in any reassignment.

**Example: decommissioning broker 6**

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Build a reassignment plan that moves every replica off one broker (rack awareness omitted for brevity)."""
import json, subprocess, sys
from collections import Counter

LEAVING = 6
REMAINING = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
BS = "broker1:9092"

# Current assignment of every topic, as JSON, via the reassignment tool's --generate (we only use "current")
topics = subprocess.run(
    ["bin/kafka-topics.sh", "--bootstrap-server", BS, "--list"],
    capture_output=True, text=True, check=True).stdout.split()
topics_json = json.dumps({"version": 1, "topics": [{"topic": t} for t in topics]})
open("all-topics.json", "w").write(topics_json)
out = subprocess.run(
    ["bin/kafka-reassign-partitions.sh", "--bootstrap-server", BS, "--generate",
     "--topics-to-move-json-file", "all-topics.json", "--broker-list", ",".join(map(str, REMAINING + [LEAVING]))],
    capture_output=True, text=True, check=True).stdout
current = json.loads(out.split("Current partition replica assignment")[1].splitlines()[1])

load = Counter(b for p in current["partitions"] for b in p["replicas"] if b != LEAVING)
moves = []
for p in current["partitions"]:
    if LEAVING not in p["replicas"]:
        continue
    # Replace the leaving broker by the least-loaded remaining broker not already in the list
    candidates = sorted((b for b in REMAINING if b not in p["replicas"]), key=lambda b: load[b])
    target = candidates[0]
    load[target] += 1
    new = [target if b == LEAVING else b for b in p["replicas"]]   # keeps position, so preferred-leader order is kept
    moves.append({"topic": p["topic"], "partition": p["partition"], "replicas": new})

json.dump({"version": 1, "partitions": moves}, sys.stdout, indent=1)
```

```bash
python3 drain_plan.py > drain-6.json
bin/kafka-reassign-partitions.sh --bootstrap-server broker1:9092 \
  --reassignment-json-file drain-6.json --execute --throttle 150000000
bin/kafka-reassign-partitions.sh --bootstrap-server broker1:9092 \
  --reassignment-json-file drain-6.json --verify            # repeat until all completed

# Verify the broker is empty: no replicas in any log directory
bin/kafka-log-dirs.sh --bootstrap-server broker1:9092 --describe --broker-list 6 \
  | tail -1 | jq '[.brokers[].logDirs[].partitions[]] | length'
# 0

# Stop it, then remove its registration from the cluster metadata
ssh broker6 'sudo systemctl stop kafka && sudo systemctl disable kafka'
bin/kafka-cluster.sh unregister --bootstrap-server broker1:9092 --id 6
```

A stopped but still registered broker appears as **fenced** in the metadata, and some tools keep reporting it. Unregistering removes it cleanly. Never unregister a broker that still hosts replicas.

**Decommissioning a controller**

Controllers hold no partition data, so there is nothing to drain. With a dynamic quorum (Kafka 3.9+), remove the voter first, then stop the node (Section 2.3):

```bash
bin/kafka-metadata-quorum.sh --bootstrap-controller ctrl1:9093 \
  remove-controller --controller-id 3 --controller-directory-id <directory-id-of-ctrl3>
```

Keep an odd number of voters (3 or 5). Removing a voter from a 3-node quorum leaves a quorum that tolerates no further failures, so add the replacement first when possible.

**Common mistakes**

| Mistake | Consequence |
|---|---|
| Shutting down before draining | Permanent under-replication until someone reassigns |
| Draining without capacity checks | Remaining brokers run out of disk or network during the move |
| Forgetting internal topics | `__consumer_offsets` and `__transaction_state` partitions stay on the broker |
| Leaving the broker in `bootstrap.servers` lists | Clients log connection errors (harmless if other entries work, but noisy) |
| Breaking rack balance | All replicas of some partitions end up in one zone |

**Key Takeaways**

- Decommissioning means drain, verify, stop, unregister, clean up. Shutting down alone leaves partitions under-replicated.
- Drain with a throttled reassignment that includes internal topics and respects racks.
- Verify that the broker holds no replicas before stopping it, and use `kafka-cluster.sh unregister` afterwards.
- Controllers are removed with `kafka-metadata-quorum.sh remove-controller`. Add replacements first.
- Tools such as Cruise Control's `remove_broker` automate the drain step.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. (Beginner) On a 4-broker cluster, use `kafka-topics.sh --describe` to list every partition that has a replica on broker 4, including internal topics.
> 2. (Intermediate) Extend the plan generator to respect `broker.rack` (no two replicas of a partition in the same rack) and to rotate the replacement position so preferred leaders stay balanced. Test it by decommissioning one broker.
> 3. **Interview question:** "You must remove 3 brokers from a 12-broker cluster this week. Describe your plan." *Hint: think about capacity on the remaining 9, the order of draining, batch size and throttling, internal topics, verification, and when exactly each broker is stopped and unregistered.*

#### Cruise Control

**Theory**

Reassignments, preferred elections, and decommissioning by hand work for a handful of brokers. On a cluster with dozens of brokers and tens of thousands of partitions, deciding **which** partitions to move **where** becomes an optimization problem with many constraints: disk capacity, network in and out, CPU, rack placement, leader balance, and minimal data movement. **Cruise Control**, open-sourced by LinkedIn, solves that problem continuously. It watches the load of every broker and partition, computes optimization proposals that satisfy a prioritized list of **goals**, and executes them as throttled reassignments and leader elections.

> Analogy: manual reassignment is rearranging furniture in a warehouse by eye. Cruise Control is a warehouse management system: it knows the weight of every box and the capacity of every shelf, follows fire-code rules (racks) first and convenience rules later, and moves boxes a few at a time while the warehouse stays open.

**Architecture**

```text
 Brokers (each with CruiseControlMetricsReporter)
     | per-partition bytes in/out, CPU, disk usage
     v
 __CruiseControlMetrics topic
     |
     v
 +----------------------------- Cruise Control service -----------------------------+
 |  Load Monitor  -> builds a cluster load model from metric samples                 |
 |  Analyzer      -> searches for an assignment satisfying goals in priority order   |
 |  Executor      -> applies proposals: throttled reassignments, leader elections    |
 |  Anomaly Detector -> broker failure, disk failure, goal violation, metric anomaly |
 |                     -> optional self-healing (runs a fix automatically)           |
 |  REST API      -> /kafkacruisecontrol/... (UI: cruise-control-ui)                 |
 +-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

**Goals**

Goals are classes evaluated in priority order. **Hard goals** must be satisfied (a proposal that violates one is rejected). **Soft goals** are optimized as far as possible without breaking higher-priority goals.

| Goal (examples) | Type | Ensures |
|---|---|---|
| `RackAwareGoal` | Hard | Replicas of a partition are in different racks |
| `ReplicaCapacityGoal` | Hard | No broker exceeds a maximum number of replicas |
| `DiskCapacityGoal`, `NetworkInboundCapacityGoal`, `NetworkOutboundCapacityGoal`, `CpuCapacityGoal` | Hard | Utilization below a threshold of each broker's capacity |
| `ReplicaDistributionGoal` | Soft | Similar replica counts per broker |
| `DiskUsageDistributionGoal`, `NetworkInboundUsageDistributionGoal`, ... | Soft | Similar resource usage per broker |
| `LeaderReplicaDistributionGoal`, `LeaderBytesInDistributionGoal` | Soft | Balanced leadership and leader traffic |
| `PreferredLeaderElectionGoal` | Soft | Leaders are the preferred replicas |

Capacity goals need to know what each broker can handle, which you declare in a capacity file (disk in MB, network in KB/s, CPU in percent):

```json
{
  "brokerCapacities": [
    { "brokerId": "-1",
      "capacity": { "DISK": "2000000", "CPU": "100", "NW_IN": "1250000", "NW_OUT": "1250000" },
      "doc": "Default for every broker: 2 TB disk, 10 Gbit/s NIC" }
  ]
}
```

**Setting it up (essentials)**

```properties
# On every broker: publish load metrics for Cruise Control
metric.reporters=com.linkedin.kafka.cruisecontrol.metricsreporter.CruiseControlMetricsReporter
cruise.control.metrics.reporter.bootstrap.servers=broker1:9092
```

```properties
# cruisecontrol.properties (abridged)
bootstrap.servers=broker1:9092,broker2:9092
metric.reporter.topic=__CruiseControlMetrics
capacity.config.file=config/capacity.json
hard.goals=com.linkedin.kafka.cruisecontrol.analyzer.goals.RackAwareGoal,\
  com.linkedin.kafka.cruisecontrol.analyzer.goals.DiskCapacityGoal,\
  com.linkedin.kafka.cruisecontrol.analyzer.goals.NetworkInboundCapacityGoal
num.concurrent.partition.movements.per.broker=5      # limits parallel moves per broker
default.replication.throttle=100000000               # bytes/s applied to moves it executes
self.healing.enabled=false                           # start with manual approval; enable later
webserver.http.port=9090
```

Use a Cruise Control release that matches your Kafka version line, and check its KRaft support notes: recent releases support KRaft clusters.

**Using the REST API**

```bash
CC=http://cruise-control:9090/kafkacruisecontrol

# Health of the cluster model and executor
curl -s "$CC/state?json=true" | jq '.MonitorState.state, .ExecutorState.state'

# Current load per broker
curl -s "$CC/load?json=true" | jq '.brokers[] | {Broker, DiskPct, LeaderNwInRate, FollowerNwInRate, NwOutRate, Leaders, Replicas}'

# Dry run: what would a full rebalance do? (dryrun defaults to true, so this changes nothing)
curl -s -X POST "$CC/rebalance?json=true&dryrun=true" \
  | jq '.summary | {numReplicaMovements, numLeaderMovements, dataToMoveMB}'

# Execute it for real, with an explicit throttle
curl -s -X POST "$CC/rebalance?dryrun=false&replication_throttle=100000000"

# Fill new brokers 7 and 8 with load, moving only what is needed
curl -s -X POST "$CC/add_broker?brokerid=7,8&dryrun=false"

# Drain broker 6 before decommissioning it
curl -s -X POST "$CC/remove_broker?brokerid=6&dryrun=false"

# Move leadership away from a sick broker without moving data
curl -s -X POST "$CC/demote_broker?brokerid=3&dryrun=false"

# Emergency stop of an ongoing execution
curl -s -X POST "$CC/stop_proposal_execution"
```

`dryrun=true` is the default on every operation endpoint, which is a deliberate safety net: you must explicitly ask for changes.

**On Kubernetes with Strimzi**

The Strimzi operator (Section 14.3) deploys Cruise Control for you and exposes rebalancing as a custom resource. You create a `KafkaRebalance`, review the proposal it computes, and approve it with an annotation:

```yaml
apiVersion: kafka.strimzi.io/v1beta2
kind: KafkaRebalance
metadata:
  name: add-brokers-7-8
  labels:
    strimzi.io/cluster: prod-cluster
spec:
  mode: add-brokers          # full | add-brokers | remove-brokers
  brokers: [7, 8]
# kubectl annotate kafkarebalance add-brokers-7-8 strimzi.io/rebalance=approve
```

**Self-healing: use with care**

With `self.healing.enabled=true`, Cruise Control reacts to anomalies on its own, for example moving replicas off a broker that has been dead for longer than a grace period. This shortens incidents but also means data moves at times nobody chose. Teams usually start with anomaly detection and notifications only, then enable self-healing for specific anomaly types (such as broker failure) once they trust the goals and capacity settings.

**Alternatives**

| Option | Notes |
|---|---|
| Manual `kafka-reassign-partitions.sh` | Full control, fine for small clusters |
| Cruise Control | Open source, most widely used, integrated into Strimzi |
| Vendor balancers (for example Confluent's Self-Balancing Clusters) | Built into commercial distributions |
| Managed services | The provider rebalances for you (Section 14.3) |

**Key Takeaways**

- Cruise Control models broker and partition load, proposes reassignments that satisfy prioritized hard and soft goals, and executes them with throttles.
- Accurate capacity files and metrics are the foundation: wrong capacities produce wrong plans.
- Always dry-run first and review data to move, then execute with an explicit throttle.
- `add_broker`, `remove_broker`, `demote_broker`, and `rebalance` cover most routine operations.
- Introduce self-healing gradually, after you trust the goals and the anomaly detection.

> **Practice**
>
> 1. (Beginner) Deploy Cruise Control against a local 3-broker cluster, wait for the load monitor to be ready, and read the `/load` output. Identify the busiest broker by network in.
> 2. (Intermediate) Add a fourth, empty broker. Compare the dry-run output of `/rebalance` with that of `/add_broker?brokerid=4`, especially the number of replica movements and data to move, and explain the difference.
> 3. **Interview question:** "What risks does enabling Cruise Control's self-healing introduce, and how would you reduce them?" *Hint: think about data movement during peak traffic, wrong capacity assumptions, flapping brokers, and which anomaly types are safe to auto-fix.*

<a id="123-monitoring-and-observability"></a>
### 12.3 Monitoring and Observability

You cannot operate what you cannot see. This section covers where Kafka's metrics come from (JMX), which of the hundreds of available metrics actually matter, how to interpret the most important health signals (under-replicated partitions and consumer lag), how to collect everything into Prometheus and Grafana, and how distributed tracing follows a single event across producers, topics, and consumers.

#### JMX Metrics

**Theory**

Kafka brokers, controllers, and clients measure themselves constantly: bytes in and out, request latencies, queue sizes, replication state, and much more. They publish these measurements through **JMX** (Java Management Extensions), the standard JVM mechanism for exposing runtime information. Every metric lives in an **MBean** (managed bean), a named object with attributes you can read locally or over the network. Every monitoring stack for Kafka, whether Prometheus, Datadog, or a vendor console, ultimately reads these MBeans.

> Analogy: JMX is the dashboard behind the panel of a car. The car measures speed, temperature, and fuel level all the time. JMX is the standard connector that any diagnostic device can plug into to read them.

**MBean names**

An MBean name has a **domain** and a set of **key properties**:

```text
 kafka.server:type=BrokerTopicMetrics,name=BytesInPerSec,topic=orders
 \__________/ \_____________________/ \________________/ \__________/
    domain        group (type)           metric name       extra tags (optional)
```

| Domain | Contains |
|---|---|
| `kafka.server` | Broker-level: replication, topic traffic, request handler pool, quotas |
| `kafka.network` | Request metrics per API, network processors, request channel |
| `kafka.controller` | Active controller and cluster-wide partition state (on controllers) |
| `kafka.log` | Log sizes, flush times, log cleaner |
| `kafka.producer`, `kafka.consumer`, `kafka.admin.client` | Client metrics, keyed by `client-id` |
| `kafka.streams`, `kafka.connect` | Kafka Streams and Connect metrics |
| `java.lang` | JVM: heap, GC, threads |

**Metric types**

Brokers use two metrics libraries for historical reasons. Their attributes differ:

| Type | Attributes | Example |
|---|---|---|
